The Honourable William Paterson,

House again in committee on Bill (No. 21) to amend and consolidate the law respecting railways.-The Minister of Railways and Canals.

I wish to call the attention of the committee to section 204 which deals with passenger traffic on railways. I think the time has arrived when this legislature ought to define what the maximum passenger rate on our railways shall be. The fact is that railways which operate in Canada and the United States carry the people for two cents a mile in the United States and when they cross the boundary they charge the Canadian people three cents a mile. For fifty years railways have been running in Canada and the standard passenger rate per mile has never been changed whereas the freight rates have been cut in two during that period. In New York State some years ago the New York Central applied for certain legislation in connection with a branch line, and the legislature consented to pass the Bill provided the passenger rate was not over two-cents a mile. That was made the rate for a small branch of the New York Central, and the company accepted it over all its line running through New York State. The same thing has happened in Michigan where the Grand Trunk passes. The legislature made it a two cent a mile passenger rate and all the railways in that state have had to accept it. In Europe passenger rates have been greatly reduced and are much lower in Europe than in America. One great object of cheap travel is that labour can move from place to place where it may obtain work. In Canada the passenger rates are altogether too high and we need not expect the North-west to be settled as it would be if passenger rates on railways were reduced. Cheap travel tends to promote business and to bind the country together. It will pay the railways to have a two cent fate because the statistics prove that if you reduce the price of anything the consumption increases, and Hon. Mr. PREFONTAINE.
so if you reduce the railway rate, travel will increase. We know that In connection with the post offices of every country, whenever you reduce the postal rate you increase the revenue and you increase the efficiency of the service. If there should be some loss to the railways by reducing the rate, and I do not admit if, that loss should be made up on the freight rates if it has to be made up at all. A large portion of our community use the railways mainly for travel and for fifty years they have had no consideration and never will until parliament steps in and compels our railways to reduce the passenger rate. It is said that the rates on the Canadian Pacific Railway cannot be interfered with because of their charter, but tiie rates on the Canadian Northern Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway can be reduced and if you fix the maximum rates on these lines at two cents a mile the Canadian Pacific Railway will have to accept it, and I believe they will be glad to accept it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Let me put the hon. gentleman in order. There is nothing before the committee. Mr. Maclean moves that we return to the consideration of clause 264.
Motion agreed to.

I call the attention of tiie House to a short editorial which appeared in the ' Farmers' Weekly Sun.' It says :
The distance from Detroit to Chicago via the Grand Trunk Railway is 319 miles, and the single fare is $6.25. The distance from Detroit to Toronto is 226 miles, and the single fare is $6.60. The reason for the lower fare to Chicago, though the distance is ninety-three miles greater, is that the legislature of Michigan has fixed the passenger rate through that State at two cents per mile, while the rate in Ontario is three cents per mile. The Grand Trunk Railway in Michigan received not one dollar of public aid. The Grand Trunk Railway in Canada received enormous loans from our government, and to-day owes us for principal and interest of loans made to it and to Ontario lines which it absorbed nearly $50,000,000. Is our our parliament doing anything to-day to secure for the people of Canada the same passenger rate over the Grand Trunk Railway as that road gives to the people of Michigan ? It is doing nothing in that direction. On the contrary, according to Hon. Mr. Prdfontaine, the Dominion government proposes to take many millions more of our money and give it to the company which charges us fifty per cent more for passenger rates than it charges our neighbours across the line.
Is it not humiliating that in this country where we have given the Grand Trunk Railway $50,000,000 of public money, they charge us three cents a mile to travel while they only charge two cents to the people of the United States who never gave them a cent ? If we are to go on in this paternal way subsidizing railroads let us take a leaf out of the book of our neighbours and let us compel the railways to carry our people

for two cents a mile. The New York Central Railway has a valuable franchise in this country in connection with the old Canada Southern and it is carrying the people of the state of New York for two cents a mile, but the moment it crosses the Canadian border it charges our people three cents. That is not creditable to this parliament and should not be allowed to continue. The ' Montreal Witness ' of a few days ago says editorially :
In connection with the foolish, not to say almost criminal, prodigality with which successive governments have given bonuses to all and sundry, especially railway and bridge promoters, a Toronto contemporary points out that half of the St. Clair tunnel which is in the state of Michigan has been assessed for the present year by the board of state tax commissioners for $1,800,000, and the tax for 1903 that has been levied upon this assessment is $24,640. On the other hand, the tax on the half of the tunnel which lies in Ontario is only $753. The railway fare over the Grand Trunk Railway on the Michigan side of the river is two cents a mile ; on the Ontario side it is three cents a mile. For the 2'23 miles of the St. Clair frontier tunnel built in Canada the Grand Trunk Railway received a subsidy of $375,000, but received no public aid for the portion which is in the United States territory. This is a little story of a kind that has been infinitely repeated, and it carries its own moral.
I intend to test this question in the House both now and later on. At a later stage of the Bill, I shall propose an amendment to the effect that the maximum passenger tariff rate shall not exceed two cents a mile. Such a rate would be in the interests of the people and of the railways and go a long way to promote the interchange of business and give the people what they are entitled to. They have a penny per mile travel all over England. In Australia and Hungary, where the railways are owned by the government, people travel at less than a cent a mile, and that has been found to pay. The experience of European countries, especially Austria and Hungary, is that every reduction in the rates has resulted in profits to the railway as well as to the people.
First-class fares ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
No, but they have a rate lower than one cent a mile, which allows labour to go wherever there is work to be had. What I repeat is that the experience of every country in Europe shows that where the government has reduced the rate of passenger travel, the result has been beneficial both to the railways and the public. There has been no agitation in the states of New York and Michigan for the reduction of passenger travel there. The great companies have accepted the reduction and find that their business has increased enormously. But people will say, New York is much more thickly populated than Ontario. My reply to this is that in New York there are many more lines of 197
railway, and each railway in that state has comparatively no more travel than any railway in Ontario. Yet not one of them has ever asked that the rate be put back to three cents or raised to any extent whatever.
Suppose you were to take a cent off the passenger rate, would you not have to add it on to the freight rates ? The railway companies have to live.

If you reduce the cost of travel you increase the income. That is proved by the post office and every public statistics where reductions have taken place. But even if it should have to come out of the freight receipts, why should not the people who travel be entitled to as much consideration as those who use the railways for the purposes of freight ? Are not the people who settle in the North-west entitled to a reasonable rate when they want to travel east. At present the rates are almost prohibitive, and that is one of the great grievances complained of in that country. I am not advocating something which has not stood the test of experience. Experience has proved that a reduction in the passenger rates works both in the interests of the railway companies and the public. It is humiliating that in this country, where we have given the railway companies so much public money and such great franchises, where we have assisted them by providing terminal facilities at our ocean ports, we should get nothing in return in the way of reduced charges for railway travel. I propose to insert a subclause to section 264 to this effect:	' The maximum
passenger travel shall not exceed two cents a mile.'
Is that two-cent rate universal in the United States ?
No, it is a matter of state control, as far as I can gather ; but all through the states of New York and Michigan, they. have a two-cent rate.
Are those rates fixed by the railway commission or are they incorporated in the Railway Acts ?

The two-cent passenger rate in New York was due to a small amendment to a single Bill which went through the legislature at Albany. There was an agreement with a certain road to carry people at the rate of two cents a mile. The New York Central Railway applied to incorporate this road with its own, and the state legislature said :	You may
take it if you will extend that two-cent rate over all your system. The New York Central Railway accepted this offer and all the other railway companies followed suit. In the state of Michigan, there is an Act of the legislature providing that every road running across that state shall eliarge a two-cent rate.

I hope the hon. gentleman, when he brings down his amendment to this Bill, will furnish the statistics on which he bases his argument. He has selected two of the most thickly populated states of the union and the most thickly populated portions of those states as an illustration of his argument. While I would like to see the rate reduced if possible to one cent a mile, we ought not to do anything which would not be reasonable, and the hon. gentleman ought to be able to inform us what induced the legislatures of New York and Michigan to reduce those rates. He ought to inform us what is the number of passengers per mile per day that is carried over railways in those states, also the payment of train hands, the cost of labour and other matters. As a matter of fact, while in the west we have higher rates for ordinary traffic, we have low rates in other respects. We have rates for immigrants coming in from the boundary line, which average about one cent per mile as far as Edmonton, over all the railways. That is a lower rate than is prevalent in the United States. Our passenger rates from Winnipeg to the east are as low as from points in North Dakota and Minnesota to the east, and any person who wants to travel east during certain seasons of the year can get a rate of about two cents per mile.

I presented the facts which the hon. gentleman inquires for to the House on a former occasion, and they will be found in ' Hansard.' My hon. friend refers to the special rates given immigrants and others. But what I want to see is a rate for general travel. There are all kinds of cut rates. The press have the privilege of travelling at a two-cent rate per mile, commercial travellers at 2J, and a great many other people get incidental reduction, but what I want is a maximum passenger rate for the ordinary individual and not a number of preferred classes. Let us have equal and equitable treatment for every one. It may be that if the railway companies to-day would cut off their passes, which they give to people who furnish them with freights, and if they would do away with the preferred rates which they give many classes, they would be able to give a general rate of two cents per mile. I have seen a good deal of railway travelling in this country, and the only man who seems to be treated without consideration is the man who pays the top fare and cannot get into a Pullman car. I have travelled considerably up and down the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway, and I have seen the way in which these companies treat the ordinary traveller who pays three cents a mile and has to get into the ordinary first-class coach. He is not treated as he ought to be. He it is who keeps up the railways, furnishing the great-Mr. MACLEAN.
est amount of traffic, and yet he has not had one iota of consideration for fifty years. As I have told you, we have cut down freight rates time and again. There is no way to secure the reduction which I propose but by putting it on the statute-book. The railways will bluff you every time; they will jolly you along one way or another. But place this on the statute-book, and I pledge my reputation for prophecy, whatever it may be, the railways will not lose a dollar. On the contrary, the reduction will be in their own interest. But they will never make this reduction unless we compel them to do so. You must do what the state of New York did. What the state of Michigan did. And the argument does not hold that the reduction benefits the railways because these are thickly populated states. In thickly populated states there are a great many railroads, while, in our own Northwest, while there is a sparse population, there is a comparatively small railway mileage.
But it makes a difference in the number of passengers per mile.

But where the passenger rates are reduced the consumption of passenger traffic- if I may use that expression-increases. Why, that is what makes the world go round in a commercial sense; it is the basis of our progress-reduce the price and you increase the consumption. We have given the Grand Trunk already $50,000,000 of the peoples' money. We have given the Canadian Pacific between $100,000,000 and $200,000,000 of the people's money. And I am told that we are to give the Grand Trunk $135,000,000 more of the people's money. And we have not got a single concession for the people who travel for all those grants. Now is the time to make a deal with the Grand Trunk, when it is proposed to give them this immense bonus. One condition of the contract with them should be that the maximum passenger rate should be two cents per mile, I have had a great deal of communication with the people of this country on one question or another that I happened to have raised in this House, but on no question have I met with so much approval and encouragement from the ordinary citizens as in regard to this question of railway travel. People want cheaper traffic and they are entitled to it, and they are not proposing
I am afraid the hon. gentleman is making light of the telephone.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The telephone is a pretty good thing too. And the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals thinks it is a pretty good thing, I believe. It is a very profitable enterprise in this country, is the telephone business. And the railroad business is profitable too. That being the case, there is no reason why this legislature should not

intervene on behalf of the people. It is our duty to intervene. And I intend to test this) House on this question both now and at a later stage, for that is what we are entitled to. It is what the people of other countries get by insisting on it, and it is a thing that we shall never get unless we put our demands squarely on the statute-book.

The hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) is great on theory, but his theories will not work out in practice. Of course, some parts of this country are thickly populated, and his theory might work out well enough there; but the great part of our country is sparsely settled and his theory could not be put in practice as affecting those portions. We are about appointing a railway commission. But, if you are going to cover all the details by the Act that we are now passings what will be left for the commission to do ? The safest thing for us to do is to leave these matters in the hands of these commisssioners. They will be in a better position

The accidental breaking of glass in the ceiling of the Chamber here interrupted the proceedings for a few minutes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Will the committee please come to order.

When the interruption took place, I was saying that, to my mind, there was not much use in appointing a railway commission if all the details with regard to the management of the railways were to be put in the Railway Bill. The hon. member for East York has cited the case of the state of New York with reference to railway rates. In that case the rates were incorporated in the Railway Act of the state. But if the hon. gentleman will take the trouble to study the facts with regard to all the states of the union, he will find out that in more than two-thirds of those states the rates are placed under the control of the railway commission of the state. So, I think we are safe in leaving the matter under the control of the commission here. While I would like to see the people get as low rates as they can, I could not support the amendment. You cannot run the railways without money. They have to pay interest, they have to pay their fixed charges, if nothing on their stock, and they have to pay their running expenses. In order to do that they must have revenue, and if you are going to take it off the passenger rate you will have to put it on the freight rate. So how much better off will the people be ? The hon. gentleman may pose as the champion of the people's rights, but When the people begin to understand that the hon. gentleman wants to take it off their collar and put it on their vest, they will see there is not much in his argument.

The hon. gentleman stated a moment ago that this might work in some of the populous states of the United 1974
States, but not in Canada. Now, if he will support me, I will make my amendment cover Ontario, Quebec and the maritime provinces only, and leave the North-west country at the present rate. Would he like to have that ? He has not answered my argument at all. I said the reduction in the passenger rate, wherever it has been tried throughout the world, results in an increase of revenue to the company, therefore the reduction will not necessarily come out of the freight rates. We could teach the railway companies something by reducing the rate on the Intercolonial, where we have the control, to two cents a mile. That would force all the competing roads to come down to the same rate.
What effect would that have?
It would make the other roads come to that rate, exactly what has happened in the state of New York.

Last year the earnings from passenger traffic on the Intercolonial were $1,770,000. If we reduce that by 334 per cent, which would be the equivalent of reducing the rate from three cents to two cents a mile, you would at once cut off $600,000. The net earnings on the road last year was $96,000. If the hon. gentleman's idea is carried out, there would result a loss on the Intercolonial of over $600,000.

The hon. gentleman need only apply that argument to the reduction of postage to see where he would land. He is a Liberal, or professes to be, and one of the doctrines which the Liberals have advocated for years in fiscal matters, is that if you reduce the price you increase the consumption, and you benefit both sides. He can talk as he likes. I am not defending a theory, I am giving evidence which has been brought out in other countries showing that where a reduction in the passenger rate has taken place there has been a corresponding increase in the revenue to make it up.
Why not reduce it down to one cent, then ?

Well, I will again refer the hon. gentleman to the Post Office Department. Formerly it cost a shilling to carry a letter, a reduction was made by steps until it got down to the penny letter, all over the empire.

It would require very careful calculation to find out what the effect of the reduction would be. That is a calculation that only the board of railway commissioners would be qualified to make, and it is one which this House is apparently disqualified to make.

It is just such a calculation as the people of New York and Michigan have made through their legislatures, and has been vindicated by results. The experiment in the post office was

made by the parliament of Great Britain and the parliament of Canada, and not by any commission. We have had fifty years' experience of three cents a mile on railroads; is the time never to come when we are to have a reduction ? Are we never to have a reasonable railroad travel in this country? The commission can study the question and report to parliament upon it. But I do not propose to give up my functions as a member of parliament to a commission. I have made up my mind on the subject, X have studied the question fully for a number of years, and I am convinced that I am right. I hope the hon. gentlemen in this House will study the question and see if they cannot get some more light on it.
If the hon. gentleman has made so many calculations, let him give them to us.

I have given them time after time. The statement I make is this, that the governments in Europe which control their railway rates have felt themselves justified in reducing the passenger rate in consequence of the experience they have acquired that reduced rates meant more traffic. The evidence is there, and the proof of the success of the experiment is that there is no agitation in any states of the union where they have a two cent passenger rate, to put up the rate. I am not doing this, as some hon. gentlemen have intimated, for some ulterior purpose ; I am bringing this subject up here in a simple, direct way. I do not want to have my motives impugned as have been done by some hon. gentlemen. I may be a little ahead of my time, but if a person is ahead of his time he has a right to be heard, even in this House, and to give a reason for the faith that is in him. I have given a reason why the House should study this question, and I have given a reason why my amendment should be made part of the Railway Act of this country.

If the hon. gentleman's theory is right that a lower passenger rate per mile would increase the earning power of the roads, how is it that the very clever men at the head of the railroads of this country have not adopted a two cent rate long ago ? The hon. gentleman appears to place his judgment above the judgment of all the railroad men of this country, because none of them appear to he convinced that they would increase the earning power of their roads by adopting a rate of two cents per mile for passengers.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Maclean moves to add a subsection to section 204, which will read as follows :
The maximum passenger tariff shall not
exceed two cents a mile.
In justice to the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean), we

must give him the credit of having persistently advocated this rate before the House, although it has been somewhat unpopular. It is one that may not meet with the approval of the railway companies, and may not meet with the approval of the majority of the members of this House ; but at least this must he said in his behalf, that so far as we can judge he is sincere in his belief that it would result in no great harm to the railway companies, and would not much affect their earnings, and at the same time it would be a substantial benefit to the travelling public. He has given data to substantiate the allegations he has made. He has quoted statistics of travel in the state of New York. Now the state of New York might be regarded as not furnishing a fair comparison for Canada because it is much more populous even than Ontario. But as the hon. member says, the travel is divided up amongst a larger number of railways, and therefore the proportionate travel in Canada would be in all probability quite as great for each as the proportion of travel even in the state of New York. But if that comparison is not thought to be fair, let us go to Michigan, with a population very much like that of the province of Ontario. It is settled in much the same way, and is not more thickly populated than Ontario. If in the state of Michigan the railway companies can carry on their operations by charging only two cents a mile, and make in pay, it seems to me their case furnishes a strong argument that the same thing could be done in the province of Ontario. I have no doubt whatever that if a reduction of one cent a mile was made on the ordinary travel, it would result in an increase of at least one-third more travel. Why are so many people deprived of the advantage of travel who otherwise would do so ? It is because of the want of means to enable them to travel. If you reduce the cost you will increase the traffic. If you reduce it one-third, you will undoubtedly Increase the number of people who will travel over the railroads. Now, take the railway from Toronto to Windsor, about 220 miles. It is stated, and I believe the statement is correct, coming from the source it does, that you pay as much to travel from Toronto to Windsor as you do from Detroit to Chicago, a distance of 290 miles. The conditions in Northern Indiana and southern Michigan are very much the same as in that portion of the country between Windsor and Toronto. The country is as thickly settled in the province of Ontario as either in northern Indiana or southern Michigan and if you look at the trains as you pass along you will find that the number travelling is very much the same. It may be said that that is an argument against my contention that if you reduce the rates there will be more travel, but if you take the time when three cents a mile was the rate you will find that the travel

was not as heavy In northern Indiana and southern Michigan as it was after a reduction was made to the extent of one cent a mile. The amount of travel is much greater on account of it. Why is it that the Grand Trunk Railway which passes through the province of Ontario charge the Ontario farmer or traveller, no matter what locality he comes from, three cents a mile, notwithstanding the fact that the road has been heavily subsidized in this country, while the same road goes across the border where it gets no assistance from the state and charges the citizen of that country only two cents a mile for the same accommodation ? Passenger traffic is not like freight; the traveller walks on the train and walks off again, and it costs the company nothing to load or unload. If a party desired to ship his goods a distance of 3,000 miles the company would give him a reduction on account of the long distance. They would not charge him the same rate per ton upon his goods as if they were shipped a distance of 100 miles. They would give a reduction on account of increased mileage, but it is not so with ordinary passenger travel. The passenger pays his three cents a mile whether he is travelling ten miles, fifty miles, one hundred -miles, or three hundred miles, while, if freight is to be carried, the railway will give a substantial reduction on account of mileage. The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals and other hon. members of this House have defended the provision in the Railway Bill giving the railway commission the right to make a distinction in the case of the transportation of freight for long distances as compared with short distances, hut, for the traveller there is no reduction made unless at certain competing points where competition between railway companies or competition between steamboats and railways compels the railway to make a reduction. This being the case it seems to me, that, while I do not think the hon. gentleman's resolution can properly apply to all sections of the country, I think it could apply to the great province of Ontario at least, which is as thickly settled as the state of Michigan or the state of New York, leaving out the great cities in these two states, and where the travel is just as great proportionately to the number of people as it is in the state of Michigan or the state of New York. There is no doubt whatever that a large proportion, if not all, of the loss sustained by a reduction of the passenger rate to the extent of one cent a mile would be made up by the increased number who would travel.

Mr. Chairman, it appears to me that if we were to fix the rate at two cents a mile and if we appoint a railway commission and the railway commission makes an investigation and finds that the earning power of the company is not sufficient, taking this reduction into consideration, to pay the fixed charges on the road
besides the running expenses, the railway commission would then have to raise the freight rates, because it would have no power to increase passenger rates. That being the case, according to the argument advanced by the hon. member for Bast Grey (Mr. Sproule) and the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) you would force the farmer who does not travel at all
He should travel.
To pay for some gentlemen down east to travel as much as they like.

Suppose that one hund-_ [DOT]red men were travelling on the railway' and that the railway company charged them $3 each, suppose they reduced that to $2 each, that would be $100 of a loss. If thirty-three more men travelled would you not make up your earnings ? You would not require to add it to the freight rates at all.
We have no guarantee that thirty-three more men would travel except the hon. gentleman's statement.
We do know this

\Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER. Each hon. gentleman should make his speech and after his speech is finished he should sit down and allow some other hon. gentleman to answer it.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Davis) asked a question and he is willing to allow me an opportunity of answering it. I was about to say that where the railway companies give special rates for certain days it is a well known fact that there is a very large increase in the amount of traffic, and so, upon the same parity of reasoning, we might eo-me to the conclusion that if you reduce the rates the amount of travel would be increased proportionately.

I am quite willing to admit that if the railway company made a special rate for one, two, or three days the public will take advantage of it, but that does not warrant us in coming to the conclusion that if you have a special rate for twelve months in the year, people are going to travel alii the time. The hon. gentleman assumes that thirty-three more men out of one hundred are going to travel, but it is only an assumption on his part. To my mind it is much better to leave this matter under the control of the railway commission. When they are seized of the facts they can come to a conclusion, and if they do come to the conclusion that it is advisable to reduce the rate to two cents a mile they will direct that such a reduction be made. That is what we are appointing them to do. We expect them to make a reasonable rate in reference to passengers and also in regard

to freight. If we were to adopt a flat rate of two cents a mile I know how it would affect the people in my part of the country. As a matter of fact there are some portions of the Canadian Pacific Railway which do not pay at all, while there are other portions of the road which pay much better, and these have to make up what the company lose on the portions that do not pay. If we reduced the earning power of the road by reducing the passenger rate on the Canadian Pacific Railway what would it mean ? It would mean that we would have a large increase perhaps in the rates on [DOT] the traffic that would ship over that road and the government, having no control over the freight rates, we would have to suffer. We paid $3,500,000 to carry the wheat last year from Winnipeg to Port Arthur. I would like to ask the hon. member for East Grey, or the hon. member for East York, how many of the producers of that wheat travel up and down the country. Virtually they do not travel at all, and those who are producing the wealth of the country would be taxed for the benefit of the gentlemen who do the travelling and who want to take a few holidays.

Do the railway statistics justify any change at all ? Iam quite willing to admit that it would be an agreeable thing to the people to be allowed to travel at two cents a mile. I suppose a larger number would be willing to travel at one cent a mile, and that the number would be increased very much more if they were allowed to travel for nothing. How would it affect the railway companies ? Take the report of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals and he says that the entire earnings of the railways from passenger traffic last year was $22,000,000 and from freight traffic $53,000,000. Suppose we reduce that $22,000,000 by reducing the amount per mile at which passengers can travel and what will be the result ? At three cents per mile the actual net earnings of the railway companies last year were $26,000,000. The capital of the companies was $1,098,000,000, so that the earnings were a little over 2 per cent on our Canadian railways. I do not think any of us would say that with an invested capital of $1,098,000,000, 2 per cent is too much. I doubt if we were engaged in the railway business we would be content with a dividend of 2 per cent, but if we reduced those earnings by reducing the rate from 3 to 2 cents a mile it would reduce the earnings to $19,000,000, or there would be a loss of one-quarter of a cent in the dividend so that the dividend would be 1J per cent. When we realize the immense sum of money it takes to build and equip a railway, and when we find what the financial results are on all our railways at the end of the year, that they actually cannot declare a dividend of more than 2 per cent, then the 3 cent rate appears to me to be comparatively small. It may appear that Mr. DAVIS.
some railways are making money on the 3 cent rate, but there is no doubt that some are losing and if the doctrine of my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) were applied the Canadian railways would be $500,000 behind last year. It may be a desirable thing to have a rate of two cents per mile but to my mind the Canadian railways cannot afford to carry passengers at a less rate than they are charging to-day.
Amendment (Mr. Maclean) negatived.
On section 279,

We were considering in connection with subclause 3 an amendment to the effect that in case the railway company discovered any fraud in the line of a shipper putting high priced freights in a car along with freights of a lower standard, the company should have the right to add 50 per cent or any other reasonable percentage, on their ordinary freight charge as a penalty upon the wrong-doer. It was suggested that if that were done one or more of the penalizing clauses should be struck out so that the shipper acting fraudulently in this manner should not be subject to the penalties named in the Act which might be enforced by a court, and also to the increased rate of freight which could be charged. I have considered the matter, and I am convinced that the effect of enabling the company to exact an additional charge for the freight in such a case, would be more deterrent than any other mode of imposing a penalty. As a matter of fact these penalties are not very much if at all enforced; the railway companies do not follow them up by complaining, and as a result the person who perpetrates this fraud escapes. This is not a question in which the railway companies are alone interested, but it is a question in which the general public and honest shippers have also great interest. Mr. Maclean in one of his reports says that this has become a very great grievance, and he thought some remedy ought be applied to stop it. Most of the shippers ship from their own sidings and it is impossible to detect this fraud in many cases so that it is often successfully perpetrated. Suppose a man is shipping one hundred barrels of flour, he might put in half a dozen barrels filled with articles which should pay) a very much higher rate. It is only occasionally that discovery is made and the opinion of persons with whom I have discussed the question is that it would be better to make the penalty higher than lower.
I do not think it would be well for us to strike out any of the other penalties, because in my opinion they are not any more severe than they ought to be. I may say that the penalties mentioned in this Act are very much lower than the corresponding penalties in tiie United States; indeed some penalties which we fix at $1,000 are $10,000 or $20,000 in the United States. If after an experi-

ence of this clause there are good reasons why it should not be continued in the law, parliament can at any time eliminate that feature of the measure.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I regret to have to take up the time of the committee in regard to this matter again, but my excuse is that it seems to strike at the very root of the principle upon which the agitation was carried on for the appointment of a railway commission. The minister has stated that this penalty is to meet extreme cases which perhaps may not occur frequently, and he has cited a case in which flour, which is shipped at a comparatively low rate of freight, might have included in that carload of flour several barrels of expensive merchandise. A condition of affairs similar to that might exist. But we all know that the railroads, not actually entirely under the law, have had inspectors in their employ for many years past for the purpose of preventing fraud of this kind ; and when we think of the watchfulness of the railways, the cleverness of their officers, the way their inspectors watch every move of the shippers, we can well understand what the hon. minister says, how impossible it would be for that to happen except in very rare cases. As the minister says, this is to meet extreme cases ; but all the shippers of the country would come under this clause and you would have all the intricacies of the classifications to deal with. 1 would like for a few minutes to draw attention to the history of the agitation which led up to the idea of a railway commission in this country. The press of the country, headed, I think I may say, by a very able journalist in Toronto, a friend of the minister for many years past, has long felt that a railway commission was necessary. That gentleman whose name I need not mention has said to me on many occasions that his aim and object was to have a railway commission appointed. He is very well informed upon the subject, and his pen has written many clever articles upon it. The whole agitation with respect to a railway commission was based upon the idea that it would be for the purpose of dealing with freight rates and freight classifications. When the first draft of this Bill was introduced into the House last year, it was a very much larger, and more extensive and more complicated measure than the present one. It was at once noticed by those who had advocated a commission that the proposed commission was for the purpose of dealing with a great number of matters which had not been agitated in the public press, and in regard to which the public had not expressed any opinion. Coming, then, to the part of this Bill which deals with the subject of tolls and tariffs, I contend that the clause which the minister wishes to add to section 3, in addition to
the penalties there named, which I do not object to, strikes at the root of the whole difficulty, or a great part of it, which we have had to deal with in this country. There have been grievances on the part of the public with respect to freight rates, and I would like to take up the attention of the House for a few minutes in reading what the public Opinion on {his question in the city of Toronto, representing the shippers of the province of Ontario, was in the year 1900. I made these observations when I had the honour of being president of the Board of Trade of Toronto, and they were endorsed unanimously by that board, not at a meeting of the council of the board, but at a public meeting of the board. I read these remarks to show what led up to this agitation with respect to tolls, classifications, &e. This is what I said :
I feel I would exceed my duties if, in the discussion of this question, I should voice sentiments which were not strictly a fair interpretation of views prevailing in this city and vicinity. It is necessary, in order to come to any conclusion with a degree of fairness, to have in view the frequent and unreasonable demands and charges made against railway corporations, resulting often in placing out of court, not only those who are guilty of such inconsistencies, but also hampering others who desire to approach matters of difference with the utmost fairness.
During the past few years there has been a noticeable tendency on the part of our railways, in order to increase their revenue, to steadily advance freight rates to the utmost limit of what it is deemed in their judgment the * traffic will stand ' ; also to withdraw from shippers privileges which they have hitherto enjoyed, and to enforce new regulations favourable to themselves, and frequently of corresponding disadvantage to shippers.
The situation has been particularly favourable to the railways, as they have enjoyed almost absolute authority in dealing with the public, who have come to look upon them largely as supreme in everything which affects their own interests.
The determination to explore a field which was beyond the jurisdiction of common carriers, resulted in bringing to the attention of the public, through the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, a discussion regarding extra rates over and above regular freight tariffs on petroleum products, and the desire to charge an extra 50 per cent under the owners' risk rule, is also illustrative of a wrong interpretation of what was expedient on the part of the railways.
The strict adherence to the most severe interpretation of every rule jointly framed by the railways, not leaving opportunities for special treatment when occasion warrants, which would exist if only one road were interested, has a tendency to cultivate a spirit of restless antipathy against the railways, which is a natural result in a democrative country like this.
I would also like to refer to the opinion of Mr. Peleg Howland, a gentleman who is at the head of the wholesale hardware firm of H. S. Howland, Sons & Company, Limited, the largest wholesale hardware firm perhaps in Toronto. He said in 1900 :

Blair,
Minister of Railways and Canals,
Parliament Buildings,
Ottawa, Out.
Dear Sir,-On the 5th inst. I wrote you a letter, under instruction from the Freight Rates Committee of the Board of Trade, complaining of a rule adopted by the Canadian Joint Freight Association, under which the railways have recently been charging 50 per cent additional for the carriage of goods more or less subject to being broken, pilfered or otherwise damaged, unless shipped at " owner's risk.' It was then pointed out how irritating this clause was to the people throughout the country, and the request was made that the matter should receive your earliest possible attention. The rule is apparently being continued by the railway companies, and the effect can only be most exasperating.
The only attention, however, that this communication has so far received is a formal acknowledgment from yourself when received, and a similar acknowledgment, received from your secretary a week ago. This matter is of the utmost importance to the whole country, and de-Mr. KEMP.
mands prompt attention, and I am instructed by the committee to again draw your attention to the character of the communication which has been forwarded to you, and to request that you should give the matter the earliest possible attention. We naturally look to the government of the country for protection from such outrageous treatment by these corporations, and if we cannot get protection through the medium which is obviously the only reasonable one to appeal the first, we will have to see what public discussion will do to arouse a proper sense in the community of the outrage that is being perpetrated, in the hope that we may in this way obtain relief.
As particularly requested in my former letter, we would like to know on what authority this rule is based. There is apparently nothing in the Railway Act to justify it. The members of our board are urging for another meeting of the committee, and the chairman is anxious to hear from you before calling the committee together.
Awaiting the honour of an early reply,
I am yours truly,
(Sgd.) EDGAR A. WILLS.
Secretary.
Dictated by Mr. Hugh Blain,
Chairman of the Committee.
The result of that correspondence was this. I do not know exactly what pressure was brought to bear upon the Minister of Railways at that time by the railway company ; but at any rate these companies saw that the idea of their being allowed to enforce a penalty of 50 per cent over and above their tolls was so unpopular that they discontinued the charge, and although the law is there, they have not seen fit to exact that penalty from shippers. This Bill was framed for the purpose of regulating tolls, and as regards subsection 3 of section 279, I may say that I am perfectly willing that the shipper should be subjected to the same penalty as the railway company. I am not objecting to that, although it must be remembered that in the old Act no such penalty exists and that there has been none against the shipper up to this particular time. The hon. minister, however, in this Bill sees fit to exact a penalty of $100 to $1,000 where a shipper falsely, with intent to defraud, bills goods in order to get a lower rate of freight than he is entitled to. I do not object to that, because that is a penalty which would be subject to the jurisdiction of the court. The shipper charged with this offence must be brought before the pi'oper tribunal and given a proper trial but to put it in the power of the railway companies-knowing, as we do, their tendency to exact fines and tolls which are unfair and illegal, knowing how impossible it is to ever get compensation from them, knowing how many shippers and thousands of dollars of claims against railway companies which it is impossible to collect- and I am talking now from personal experience-knowing all these things. I say that to put in a clause of that character just in order to meet a few extreme cases is most unfair. We know the difficulty of making a proper classification and the lia-

bility of clerks to make mistakes. There is not one shipper in five hundred who has ever seen this classification which is made by the railway companies. It was never submitted to the public for consideration. The railway companies never asked the public to pass upon it. In this book there are three thousand different items, and not one shipper in five hundred has ever seen the book. So that every day there are chances of misunderstandings and mistakes which are not wilful. There are, however, opportunities for dishonest men to evade the law, and these should come under the section which provides a penalty of from $100 to $1,000 to be inflicted by the courts ; but to give a railway company, in addition to that, the power to collect of its own motion a penalty for the improper classification of freight according to the law which they made themselves-to enable them to inflict a penalty of 50 per cent in addition to the regular freight rate in such cases, is an outrage. I have already drawn the attention of the hon. minister to the fact that this classification has not been authorized by the Governor in Council, and the hon. minister referred to it as an unjustifiable step on the part of the railway company.
I referred to their issuing it without authority.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The hon. minister deserves a great deal of credit. He has shown a great deal of courage. He has taken great pains in preparing this Bill. I have admired the stand he has taken. He has not allowed himself to be put aside by either the railway companies or the shippers or the public, and he evidently intends to treat the public fairly ; but the public have not had facilities for reaching the ear of the minister to the same extent as the railway companies. In the brief of the railway companies, this very principle I am discussing is plainly put forward. Here is the report which the representatives of the railway companies put before the minister some weeks ago. They distinctly point out in their memorandum No. 1 some of the matters over which the board should not have jurisdiction. Among these are claims against the companies to recover back tolls alleged to be improper, claims for improper discrimination in the carriage of traffic, and for breaches of various provisions respecting tolls, and claims of the companies against the shippers. That is the stand they take, and it is an unreasonable one. I do not object to the shipper being subjected to a penalty for false billing, but I object to him being made subject to a double penalty. If this Bill passes, I expect that the commission will be appointed. It will not be very long before we have another session. As soon as the commission is appointed, let it take up this question of classification. The people will then have a tribunal before which they can come, such
as they never had before, and they can there submit their views with respect to classification. But to say, as is done by this amendment, that this classification, in regard to which the public have never been heard, shall not only be binding on the shipper, but have attached to it this unreasonable proposition is not right. If the hon. minister could hear the views of the merchants and shippers all over the country, in every town and village, he would see the force of my plea. How many of these classifications are distributed throughout the country ? Not one shipper in five hundred has ever seen one of them. Yet every shipper is to be bound by it. Taking all the circumstances into consideration, I hope that the hon. minister will not insist upon his amendment. If next session he should find that it is necessary to provide for a double penalty against the shipper, then let him bring forward a provision to that effect. But now, with the reform already effected, let us pause until the public have an opportunity to be heard.

I understand that the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Kemp) objects to the amendment that has been proposed, on the ground that the fine is sufficient and that the double penalty should not be charged.
Yes.

As I read this section, it seems all right. It is directed against the man who by means of false billing, false classification, false report of weight or any other means shall ' knowingly, wilfully, or shall willingly suffer or permit any person or persons to obtain transportation for goods at less than the regular toll ' and subjects him to a penalty of not more than $1,000, nor less than $100. And the amendment provides, in addition, that the shipper shall be subject to double the rate of the freight to be charged. It seems to me that any one who is guilty of the crimes mentioned, false billing, false classification, false report of weight, and who wilfully tries to impose upon the railway by these means can hardly be subject to too heavy a penalty. The case mentioned by the hon. member for East Toronto, of a clerk not knowing the classification, and making a mistake would not come under this section at all, for the offence must be wilful, and must have for its object the defrauding of the company before the clause can apply. I do not think the penalty provided by the section and the amendment is too heavy, because one guilty of such acts should be most severely punished.

Might I explain to the hon. member for West York (Mr. Campbell) a matter with regard to which I do not think he sees as I do. I may not be able to make it clear, but I will try. As I said, and as he understands, I do not object to the section

as it stood originally, but what I object to is the double penalty which can be exacted by the railway company without reference to the commission. One accused under subsection 3, as it stands, comes within the jurisdiction of the commission, or a magistrate to be tried. But under the amendment, it is left in the power of the railway company to seize the goods. They are as likely to make mistakes as a shipper is,-perhaps more so. And yet, without the intervention of a magistrate or any other tribunal, the company would be in a position to exact the penalty, for they have control of the goods. And even though they might be wrong, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Campbell) knows how difficult it is to get a refund from railways when the money is once in their Ciands. If the shipper were brought before a magistrate, or before the commission to have the case tried and decided, it would not be so serious. But under this amendment, it is left to the railway company to decide the ease without the intervention of any court.

This amendment is in the interest of the honest shipper. Suppose two men doing business side by side ; one ships his goods properly and the other makes a false classification. In such a case the dishonest man has a great advantage over the honest man. For that reason I am in favour of the amendment proposed. As has been pointed out, the section does not affect the man who makes a mistake, therefore the argument of the hon. member for East Toronto on that point is to be set aside. That hon. gentleman says that very few men ever saw this classification. It is not necessary for the shipper to see the classification all he has to do is to correctly describe his goods and the classification is made for him. If he has correctly described his goods, there can be no penalty and he cannot be made liable. This is meant for people who, for instance, describe loaded cartridge shells as bolts and nuts, or pickles in glass and baking powder and spices as vinegar and coffee; electric goods as hardware ; liquors as canned goods, and so on. It is intended to meet the case of men who send out a carload described as hay, but which includes smoked meats and other commodities, or a carload described as settlers' effects, afterwards found to contain over a hundred packages of groceries and hardware, that under true classification would have added over $128 to the freight. These are the men we are trying to get at, and we are doing it in the interest of the honest shipper. These false descriptions of goods are by no means of rare occurrence. The complaint is general from one end of the country to the other. And. for my part, if one of the penalties is to be dropped, I would rather drop the thousand dollars and keep the penalty provided for in the amendment, for it is quick Mr. KEMP.
in its operation and will do more in a month to check the evil complained of than the other will do in years. For the railway company would be very slow to proceed to enforce a fine or penalty against one of its customers. It would sooner suffer the loss than do so, especially where there is strong competition. If we were only trying to protect the railway company, we might leave the section as it stands, feeling that if the railway companies do not look after their own interest, the fault is their own. But we are trying to protect the honest shipper against the dishonest shipper. And I do not see why any of us should feel bound to stand up here and advocate the rights of men who wilfully describe their goods wrongly in order to get a cheaper rate of freight than they are entitled to.

My hon. friend (Mr. Kemp) makes the point that(this thing can occur but seldom, and that we are establishing a principle of a serious character when there is no real need for our doing so. I do not know what my hon friend's information on that question may be, but I would not think he had wide knowledge unless he had taken pains to inquire of the railway companies on the subject. But I can point out to him that Mr. McLean, whose business it was to make very careful inquiry into all matters of railway interest when he was advising us on the subject of a railway commission, and who had no particular leaning,
I presume, either for or against the railway companies, felt it his duty to advise us that this was a grievance of very considerable magnitude, that it was attracting a great deal of attention, and that honest shippers were very desirous that, so far as possible, protection should be afforded them against dishonest shippers. My hon. friend has read some instances to give the committee an idea of the nature of this sort of fraud. I am told that the cases are of very frequent occurrence indeed, that the tendency is growing, and that it needs to be stopped, not in the interests of the railway company alone-though they might fairly, as a matter of justice, apply to this parliament to put means into their hands whereby imposition and fraud upon them could be prevented-but in the interests of the business community at large. We may well consider that interest as paramount, and one that we. ought to serve. I am surprised to hear from my hon. friend that this suggestion is unpopular in Toronto and meets with such indignation. I cannot conceive that any body would be offended or dissatisfied with this legislation if he were an honest shipper ; and I am sure my hon. friend is not doing justice to the business people of Toronto when he says that there is such widespread dissatisfaction with this proposal. I think the hon. gentleman would find that even in Toronto the business men would be pre-

pared to support any legislation which would prevent this class of fraud from being perpetrated. It is a monstrous wroug upon honest men that this thing should go on. I think I made out my case clearly when I spoke to the committee before, and the hon. gentleman did not succeed in answering it. I showed that it is an extremely difficult thing for the railways to follow it up. They may open the barrels, or boxes, or cases, when they are shipped at some central point, or some large station where they have a large staff of clerks. But even then they could only examine an occasional box, or barrel, or package, even in those large centres where the cars are loaded. But when the cars are loaded at a remote point, or on private sidings alongside the factory or warehouse, they cannot follow up the fraud. At best they can only have inspection made of a limited number of packages, so as to test the character of the whole.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: In regard to remote sidings as the hon. gentleman mentioned, will he not admit that at remote sidings there are riot usually merchants who carry on an extensive business, and consequently it is not likely that expensive hardware would be put into a carload of hay or flour ? It is not at these points that the railways have agents and inspectors.

Granted, but the hon. gentleman must remember that if you take a carload of boxes or barrels it would not be possible to have an inspection that would cover anything more than a sample here and there. But we know, if there is a deliberate purpose to defraud, with what ingenuity the shipper will place his goods or his packages so as if possible to remove suspicion. At the very best therefore the company cannot make anything but a limited inspection of the goods that are being forwarded. I think the bon. gentleman is in error when he speaks about the dissatisfaction among business men. He has referred to the facts connected with the issue of that freight classification, and the difficulties which they complain of as to changes in tbe classification. No doubt there has been a great deal of dissatisfaction in the classification, with the manner perhaps in which it is done, with the way in which they put out these freight classifications without authority. But that is a totally different subject. There is no connection between the classification and these persons who are perpetrating frauds, except in a very indirect way. Nobody need make any mistake about the classification. The shipper has it entirely in his own hands to make the shipment properly, to bill tbe goods in accordance with the classification. There is no reason why he should complain of this clause, or of the penalties which it is proposed to impose upon the fraudulent shopper. If he wants to do business honestly it is much easier for him to act honestly than dishonestly. The subject of classification is one which we have thoroughly dealt with in this Bill. The hon. gentleman will remember that the board have entire control of the subject. I think I can safely say that iu no legislation which has been passed in any state of the neighbouring republic have they got the same comprehensive grasp of the matter of classification as we have here. Now the hon. gentleman seems to think that an innocent shipper coming into this country would be subjected to these penalties. There is no reason for any such fear. A man must have an intent to perpetrate a fraud, or else he is not subject to the additional toll. We could not safeguard the innocent shipper any better than we have done. I take it that nobody can possibly complain of this proposed amendment who does not sympathize with men who wish to act dishonestly. It is not in the interest of the public at large that people should be afforded an opportunity of committing fraud, or that they should be free from penalties when they do commit fraud upon railway companies any more than if the fraud was committed against a private individual.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: May I ask the minister a question as to how this extra penalty will be collected ? Does the hon. minister claim that under this amendment a man will be tried before a magistrate or the commission? Or does he understand, as I understand, that the company may act arbitrarily, and that they may be able to collect this additional amount the same as the ordinary freight rate before the goods are delivered ?
The hon. gentleman is not referring now to the penalty which we are imposing.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am satisfied with the original penalty.

If the railway company discovers that any person has been billing falsely, or has been shipping iu the fraudulent way which has been described, they may make a demand upon the shipper to pay this extra fifty per cent advance upon the toll, and the shipper would be obliged, if he wanted to get his goods at once, to pay that fifty per cent on receiving them. He would not need to resort to legal proceedings to get the goods, or to compel the surrender of the goods to him by the company if he paid that amount. But having paid that amount under protest, he then has several courses open to him from which he can choose. If he did not wish to take any legal proceedings against the railway company to recover that amount, he could apply to the board of railway commission-i ers and the board would have power to

make an order to compel ttie refund of that amount. All he would suffer would be the temporary deprivation of that extra fifty per cent, if he were wrongfully charged with fraud. Then he might have another remedy.
