speakeroldname: Mr. L. P. DEMERS (St. John and Iberville).
speechtext:
I beg to move the following amendment :
Whenever damage is caused to any lands and fences, plantations or buildings and their contents by fire started by a railway locomotive, the company making use of such locomotive shall be responsible for such damage and may be sued for the recovery of such damage in any court of competent jurisdiction.
The amendment of the Minister of Railways does not change the law as it stands now. It only changes the law as to the evidence, but not as to the responsibility of the company. The purpose of my amendment is to change the law as to the responsibility of the company. Under the amendment of the minister, although it may be proved that the company started the fire and burned the property, they are not responsible if they bring their own employees and prove that their locomotives were properly constructed. The House will see at once that the position of the farmer or the proprietor who has suffered from the fire is very precarious under such a law, and that it would be unwise for him to bring up a lawsuit against the company under such conditions, because the result would depend upon the evidence which is in the hands of the defendant. As I have already explained to the House when I moved last session, and this session the second reading of my Bill, this very same question has been brought up in the Imperial House of Commons. In 1900, a Bill similar to the amendment I now move was presented to the Eng-

lish House of Commons and in spite of the opposition of the leader of the House, such was the feeling in England on this matter, that the second reading of that Bill was carried by a vote of 303 against 80. I do not know why this measure has not since become law in England, if it be not on account of the delay in parliamentary procedure there. Whatever be the case, we are not obliged to wait in Canada until the English people have adopted such a law if we once come to the conclusion that it is a proper law for us to enact here. I hold that the railway companies are enjoying a privilege in this respect which they should not enjoy. I find that according to common law of all the provinces the railway companies are responsible. The Privy Council in the case of Roy vs. the Canadian Pacific Railway has decided that the common law of England and the common law of France, which we follow in the province of Quebec, are similar on this point, and that it is only because the power of parliament is supreme that railway companies are not responsible in such a case. Judge Blackburn, in the case of Jones vs. Festiniog Railway Company, said :
The general rule of common law is correctly given in Fletcher v. Rylands, that when a man brings or uses a thing of a dangerous nature on his own land he must keep it in at his own peril, and is liable for the consequence if it escapes and does injury to his neighbour. Here the defendants were using a locomotive engine with no express parliamentary power making lawful that use, and they are therefore at common law bound to keep the engines from doing injury ; and if the sparks escape and cause damage. the defendants are liable for the consequence, though no actual negligence be shown on their part.
This is very clear. If you use a locomotive, and if parliament has not given you that special power, though its use may be perfectly lawful, and though the locomotive may be as perfect as it can be, though you have not been negligent at all according to the common law of England and also of France, you are responsible if you cause damage to another. This is the principle of common law, based upon the Roman law, that you must not cause any damage to another, that you must not make a use of your property so as to interfere with the rights of others. The railway companies [DOT]have the right to the enjoyment of their property, their track and their lands, but they have not the right to injure the property of their neighbours. They have no more right to throw sparks on the land of another than any one has a right to throw stones on the property of his neighbour. This same measure was brought into the English House of Commons in the session of 1900, and that House expressed its approval of it by a vote of 303 to 80. I think this amendment should be adopted for the protection of the farmers, and all who wish that the railway companies shall not be put above the common

law of this country should vote iu favour of it. This is the proper time, when we are revising the Railway Act. If this law is not adopted to-day, it will he adopted later on, there is no doubt about it, but it may take some years.

1 heartily concur in the remarks that have been made by the hon. member for St. John and Iberville (Mr. Demers). I think his amendment should be adopted, because, as he has said, even in England, public opinion is ripe for such a change in the law. I have read very carefully the debates which took place in the House of Commons in England, in 1900 when this law was proposed there, because I was personally interested in the case of Roy vs. the Canadian Pacific Railway, which went before the Privy Council. I do not see why this parliament, when granting special privileges to railway companies, should not bind them to respect, not the privileges, but the rights by common law of the riparian proprietors. When a locomotive emits sparks and causes injury to neighbouring lands or houses or barns, the company should be liable in damages for such injury. I therefore concur heartily in the remarks made by my kon. friend, and I hope that the House will agree to this amendment. If it does not pass this year, it will come up every session until we have the principle sanctioned by this parliament, that the railway company shall not enjoy any special privileges as regards this very important matter.

The amendment which was moved by me is to the effect that the company shall be obliged to disprove negligence. It is very difficult to prove negligence against a railway company under such circumstances, so much so that people who have suffered damage for loss in this way, as a general rule fail to secure any redress from the company, because they have no means of establishing by proof that the company failed to use the best and most modern appliances and equipment for the purpose of preventing sparks flying from their locomotives. Therefore, the principle which governs has been modified to this extent, that the company shall be liable for fires caused by sparks from locomotives in the event of their failing to prove that they were not guilty of negligence either as to the way in which they used their locomotive or as to the condition in whicli the locomotive was. My hon. friend proposes to revolutionize the law and the principles which govern altogether. He proposes to have it enacted that wherever a railway company traversing the country causes a fire to take place, no matter how innocently, no matter how fully the company may have complied with [DOT] every condition and every requirement of the law they shall, because they caused the
fire, make good the damage. The principle of the common law, as my hon. friend stated, is this, that when parliament incorporates a railway company and authorizes it to run railway trains, it necessarily implies that the company may exercise, if it does so properly, the powers which have been Conferred upon it by law ; and if, in the lawful exercise of such powers, it necessarily does damage to anybody, that damage follows as a necessary consequence of the lawful exercise of that power, and therefore the company should not be liable to make it good. That is the principle of the common law, and that principle I would not feel just now like recommending the committee to deviate from.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am in favour of the amendment proposed by my hon. friend from St. John and Iberville (Mr. Demers). When this matter was up before, I stated my views. Until the judgment of the Privy Council in the Canadian Pacific Railway vs. Roy, I always entertained the opinion that section 288 of the Railway Act (1888), covered the case, and that, in the province of Quebec at all events, railway companies were responsible for the damages which they caused through the loss of buildings by fires caused by sparks from their engines.
That was the universal jurisprudence until that decision.

Yes, and I think that that jurisprudence was justified by the provisions of section 288 :
Company not Relieved from legal Liability by Inspection or anything done hereunder.
No inspection had under this Act, and nothing in this Act contained, and nothing done or ordered or omitted to be done or ordered, under or by virtue of the provisions of this Act, shall relieve, or be construed to relieve, any company of or from any liability or responsibility resting upon it by law, either towards Her Majesty or towards any person, or the wife or husband, parent or child, executor or administrator, tutor or curator, heir or personal representative of any person, for anything done or omitted to be done by such company, or for any wrongful act, neglect or default, misfeasance, malfeasance or nonfeasance, of such company, or in any manner or way to lessen such liability or responsibility, or in any way to weaken or diminish the liability or responsibility of any such company, under the laws in force in the province in which such liability or responsibility arises.
In the province of Quebec it has been a subject of contention whether a railway, exercising a trade which is of a dengerous character, was responsible for damages, and the weight of opinion was that, under the French law-which provides that any person who exercises a calling or trade of a dangerous character does so at their own risk and is responsible for the damages, whether the most modern appliances were used or not, and whether or not everything was done to prevent accidents-the railway I companies were responsible. The simple

fact of exercising a trade which is dangerous makes the person exercising it responsible for all damages resulting from the exercise of such trade. He exercises it at his own peril, irrespective of the question whether he shows negligence or not. Under that principle of the French law, coupled with the provision of section 288, which says that nothing shall diminish the liability or responsibility of any company under the laws of the province where such responsibility or liability exists, the railway companies, in the province of Quebec, were held responsible for the damages caused by sparks from their engines. That jurisprudence was set aside by the decision of the Privy Council in the Canadian Pacific Railway and Roy.
The Privy Council said that their decision was according to the law in the province of Quebec.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Quite so, and for that reason 1 think that the time has come when this parliament should accept the principle which in my opinion governs in the French law, and make the railway companies responsible for the accidents due to the dangerous nature of their operation, irrespective of the question of negligence. When a company is exercising a dangerous occupation, it is doing so for its own benefit, and not for the benefit of the public. In fact, in many instances, these railways are a detriment to the public and particularly to the farmer. It is no advantage for a farmer to have his land cut up by a railway and be subjected, from one end of the year to the other, to all the inconveniences which follow the operation of a railway ; and therefore it seems to me that when damage is caused, it should be paid by the person who benefits from the operation of the thing causing the damage. In ninety-nine cases out of a hundred, it will be impossible for a farmer to establish negligence on the part of the railway company, and wiry should he be compelled, not only to put up with the annoyance of having a railway pass through his property, but also with the risk of having his buildings destroyed by fire and the loss which such fires may cause to him. It seems to me that the amendment is justified by law and equity and should be enacted, particularly at preseni, when railways are so numerous and the danger from fire has so increased. In dealing with matters of this kind, it is well to know what has been done elsewhere. In England the feeling has grown very largely that railway companies should be made liable for every accident due to their operation. In 1900, a measure was submitted in the Imperial House of Commons to this effect, which passed Its second reading but did not go any further.
Never heard of it since.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Possibly, but the hon. gentleman knows how diflicult it is in the Imperial House of Commons to have a measure of this sort adopted. In any event, there was a very large majority of the House voted for the second reading in 1900.
A majority of those present at the time.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I take it that the fact that the second reading was voted by a large majority is pretty good evidence that the feeling of the House was in favour of the Bill ; and the fact that it did not become law is no answer to my contention. At all events, I give this fact to the committee for what it is worth, and I am not one of those who think that we should adopt or refuse to adopt legislation simply because a precedent has been set in either respect elsewhere. I base my support for this amendment on the ground that it is based on a good principle in law, which is to-day sanctioned by many courts in the British colonies, as for instance in cases where damages are caused by the operation of a nuisance. Take the case of a sawmill operated in a city. It has been frequently held that the people in the neighbourhood are entitled to damages caused by the vibration and smoke, and in many instances people have been granted injunctions to restrain corporations from exercising businesses of that sort. Take the case of a livery stable in the city of Montreal.
The case of Drysdale ?

Yes, Mr. Drysdale had a livery stable on St. Denis street which is an important residential section of the city, and he was restrained by the courts from carrying on his business because of the bad odour from the stable.
Is there any analogy between that case and the present one ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Yes, there is this analogy that in each case the parties are carrying on a business which is dangerous or a nuisance, and should either be restrained from doing it or be made responsible.
But parliament gave a charter to the railway company which it did not do to Mr. Drysdale.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Quite true, but if the railway company, in the exercise of its functions, causes damage, why should it not be responsible ? The principle is as old as the hills, as old as the Roman law. that you must not use your property so as to cause damage to others. There is no principle in law which has been more universally adopted by all civilized countries than this, and it seems to me that the amend-

ment of my bon. friend from St. John's and Iberville is based upon that principle.
Mr. McCarthy. I think that the effect of the amendment of the hon. member foist. John's and Iberville will be to alter the law as it has existed for years.
Not at all. It will be reverting to the law.

That may be the case in the province of Quebec, but the highest Court of Appeal has declared that its judgment in Roy and the Canadian Pacific Railway was according to the law as it has always existed in the province of Quebec and elsewhere. I am unable to see any injustice in the law as it stands, and as it has been interpreted by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, and I think it is much better to leave the law as it has been settled by that court. It is very desirable that there should be stability in our laws and jurisprudence, and I think we should hesitate before unsettling what the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council has decided.

I am in favour of this amendment. I believe that we should have a universal law throughout the Dominion with regard to this matter. It was quite clear that the judgment of the Privy Council, in the case of Roy and the Canadian Pacific Railway, contradicts what, hitherto had been declared by our courts to be the law in the province of Quebec and to be what the legislature of that province intended, and in that sense this judgment operates injustice to that province. It is equally unjust to the province of Ontario because each province ought to enjoy the same rights.
I hope my hon. friend does not understand me to mean that this amendment should apply only to the province of Quebec 1

It is generally conceded in the province of Quebec that the law as it is now is unjust to the people of that province. In other words, if that province had the power to make the law they would make it different from what we have made it. I can see the justice of that so far as the province of Quebec goes, and I can see the fairness of the law to be put into effect here and practically rescind or repeal the law of the Dominion as declared by the decision of the Privy Council. There is another reason why I think it Would be well for the railway companies themselves to have the law changed in this way. Under the amendment proposed by the Minister of Railways and Canals the onus is simply put upon the railway to prove that they were not negligent. In that case all they would have to do would be to call experts-and they have plenty of them always at hand-to show that they 198
are using the best appliances, and that, therefore, there was no negligence-
Mr. McCarthy. May I ask the hon. gentleman a question ? Would that satisfy the amendment of the Minister of Railways and Canals ? Would it not be necessary for them to call the servants or employees Who were in charge of the engine at the time ?

That is partly what they would do, of course. I was trying to see how this would work out practically in court, for that is what we must do here-find out how the parties' rights would work out in court if there was a fire and the party damaged brought action. First, the railway company would bring in experts to prove that the engine was made in the best way. Then they would call the fireman and engine driver to show that the proper appliances were on the engine and all that kind of thing. That is, the company would call the employees who are interested in showing that they had carried out the Instructions given them. I am not going to suggest that these employees would perjure themselves, but, of course, they would not be likely to notice their own negligence. And, as any evidence on the other side Would have to depend upon a knowledge of facts within control of the company, the 'judge would simply have to decide on the weight of evidence though it might not necessarily be evidence clearly true. Besides, if it is not well settled that the railway must pay under any circumstances, the effect will be that the railways that do the best they can to avoid fires will be paying for railways that are careless. In this way :	If it were fairly settled and fairly
understod by judges and arbitrators settling the damages to be paid to landowners for land taken for the construction of the railway, that a man could not necessarily recover for damage to property or buildings due to sparks from the locomotives-if it were fairly understood that negligence must be proved before damages could be recovered in such cases-that fact would have to be taken into consideration and allowed for the landowner when his lands Were being taken. It would be just the same as with the drainage law. If the works of the company interfere with the drainage and so injure the property, that fact is taken into consideration and damages are allowed. Whether the damage is from water or from fire, the railway is the cause of the damage, and there should be an allowance in one case as in the other. And, if the farmer cannot recover piece by piece as the damage from fire occurs-if he is not paid by the job, so to speak-he must re-eovet in a lump sum for the danger he is likely to be subject to. In that case, a careful company, one not likely to cause one-tenth as many fires as another would, yet have to pay just as much in damages



as a.more careless company, for the arbitrators would have no means of differentiating between companies in that way and would be obliged to make allowance for this prospective damage on the basis of common experience and allow it as compensation when the lands are taken. But if we settle it that companies are to pay as they burn up crops or effect other injury by fire, this element would be eliminated in assessing the damage of lands through which the railway runs. And so it would be sound legislation to enact clearly that the companies are to be responsible absolutely for the damage they do in the way suggested by the hon. member who moved the amendment. That amendment would be preferable to the bne proposed by the minister.

I do not wish to prolong this discussion, but I have a "word or two to say in favour of the amendment proposed by the hon. member foist. John's and Iberville (Mr. Demers). The farmers of my county, and, I suppose of every county, lose heavily every year by fires caused by locomotives. And it is almost impossible to get anything from the company. And, if you go into court to *prove that the fire was due to the negligence of the company's employees, you must risk all your property in the attempt, for, when they are sued by a farmer in such a case, the railway company carry the case from court to court to defeat him. A farm-'er's whole property is placed in jeopardy if he attempts to recover damages, no matter how clear it may be that the fire was due to sparks from the locomotive. Something 'should be done to compel the railway companies to be careful, and, when they are not careful, but burn down our crops, fences and buildings, they should be compelled to pay. In the county of Kent only last sum-Iner, I saw from four to five acres of standing timber and a field of grain burning: The farmer could not prove that the fire originated from the railway engine, though everybody knew that that was the cause of it. The consequence was that the farmer had to suffer the loss. I think the Minister of Railways ought to take up this matter seriously and consent to this amendment moved by the hon. member for St. John's and Iberville (Mr. Demers).

I would not have risen to speak if the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Robinson) who is a layman, had not set me an example by speaking' before I did. It is not my intention to deal with the legal aspect of the question, but taking a broad common sense view of it. I quite agree with the remarks of those who favour the amendment. It means simply this, that if any man who is engaged in an occupation caused damage, he should pay for the damage. I sympathize with those legal gentlemen who have spoken about the difficulty of proving their case Mr. LANCASTER.
from the employees of the defendant. I have had some experience in that line in a case that happened some time ago. In my own village a young lawyer had brought a case before the court, and the only person he had to examine was the defendant. After the defendant was examined he said : Your honour, that is my case. The judge was an older practitioner than the young lawyer ; he leaned over the desk and said to him : I will give you some advice, always be vei-y careful in taking a case where you have got to rely entirely on the evidence of the defendant. I think that is a good principle of law, at least it is a common sense view. I think people who suffer damage from a railway ought to be very careful in taking a case where they rely altogether upon the employees of the defendant, who would be the parties who caused the damage if they had left their smokestack open, or something of that kind. Other countries are looking into this matter as well as Canada. In the United States, that country which has so many railways and which takes such precautions in the in-tei-est of the people, we find that the states of Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, Wisconsin and South Cai-olina, have adopted laws similar to the amendment which the hon. member for St. Johns and Iberville is introducing. I was proceeding to say that there seems to be an impression on the part of some hon. members that the amendment moved by the hon. member for St John's and Iberville affects to change the principle of the common law. Now, my impression from the little reading 1 have been able to do on this line, is that the amendment does not depart from the common law at all, but simply reaffirms the principles of the common law of England as it exists to-day, and I do not understand that it differs in this respect from the civil law of old Rome. So, I think we are entirely one, both civilians and common law lawyers, on the point that if a man brings a peculiarly dangerous object on his land the effect of which is to do some damage to his neighbour, he is liable for the damage to his neighbour no matter how prudently he may have behaved, what precautions he may have taken, or how entirely clear of negligence, culpable or otherwise he may prove himself to be. My hon. friend from Colchester will remember the learned article of Sir Frederick Pollock in the * Law Quarterly Review,' which he afterwards embodied in his work or torts, in which he entered into the whole question largely upon the basis of the case of Fletcher vs. Rylands to show how clearly it was the case that if a man brought an object of a dangerous character upon his land and his act resulted in injury to his neighbour he was liable for the injury so caused. I would like to quote a brief extract from Sir Frederick Pollock's book, and his words show that the decisions have clearly covered the very point now in controversy :
The decisions of our own time have settled that one who brings fire in dangerous proximity to his neighbour's property, in such ways as by running locomotive engines on a railway without express statutory authority, or bringng a traction engine on the highway, does it at his own peril.
So, if a railway company, instead of being a corporation with a charter from parliament and having express statutory authority to run locomotives upon its railway were an individual and undertook to run locomotives without such statutory authority, and damage resulted to the property of adjacent owners, it would undoubtedly be liable. An individual running a locomo-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
five train across his own property would certainly be liable if damage were caused by sparks from the locomotive, no matter how carefully he ran the locomotive, no matter what screens he used, no matter what devices he employed or what precautions he adopted. So, it is not by virtue of the common law that railway companies are enabled to do this with impunity, it is because they are empowered by statute, and thus they have express authority to do these things. If a statute which incorporates a company gives them power to run locomotives we do not infringe that permission if we say they shall run them under the limitations that would apply to a private individual if he wanted to do the same thing. So the hon. member for St. John's and Iberville is simply asking to apply the common law of England and the civil law which is the same to this proposition of running the engines of these companies. The common law does superadd to this that in spite of the express authority given to railway companies, if they do not run tbeir engines in a careful manner, if they run them in a negligent manner, they are liable, in spite of the express authorization given to them to run the locomotives. The common law it is which gives the right of action, the statute law it is which gives the immunity where it is enjoyed by a railway company. The law, then, will be as we choose to make it, and it is a matter of ethics that we shall make it, a matter of common fair play, and justice. It is open to us to make it what we please, but, of course, it is our duty to make it square with the requirements of justice and the public welfare. Now, it may be argued that when we incorporate "railway companies and give them power to run engines and trains, we do so, not for tbeir benefit merely, but for the benefit of the public at large, and it may be said that necessarily, in some instances, in spite of all diligence, in spite of the use of the best appliances on the railway, somebody's property must be injured. It is plausible to argue that in such a ease you must simply let the damage lie where it falls. But let us consider this case in its simplest form by taking as an example the Intercolonial. For the benefit of the public generally, the government runs the Intercolonial for hundreds of miles from Montreal to Halifax. Now, it may happen that, no matter what precautions are taken, somebody's property is going to be injured. If some poor man's crop is damaged or his house burned down because of inevitable accident as a result of the operation of the line, ought the damage to be borne by the poor man whose property has been injured or by the general public ? I say there cannot be any question about that "; the public at large, the government of the Dominion should pay that man for the damage caused and the injury done to him in the prosecution of an object that is being prosecuted

for the benefit of the whole country. If that is true in the case'of the Intercolonial, I cannot see why we should not pursue the analogy in the case of all companies we incorporate. The public at large should in one shape or other bear the loss. That is to say, the railway companies would have to be responsible. If the railway companies are made responsible, they will assess the cost upon the public in the charges they make, and, in the last analysis, it will be the public that will bear the burden.

I have always been told that the underlying principle of the British constitution is that parliament is supreme. If parliament is supreme when it grants privileges and rights to the railway companies I do not see why it should not equally be supreme in protecting individuals. It has been hinted this afternoon that the amendment now proposed by the hon. member for St. John's and Iberville had the effect of over-riding the common law by the civil law of Quebec. That is a mistake. 1 have here the report of the Privy Council in the famous case of Boy vs. The Canadian Pacific Kailway. Here is the judgment of the Privy Council, as given by Lord Cairns :
This permission, of course, does not authorize the thing to be done negligently or even unnecessarily to cause damage to others. Much was argued by the learned counsel for the respondent as to the peculiar jurisprudence of Quebec : but in truth there is no such difference between the law of England and the law of Quebec in this respect, as he seemed to suppose. The law of England, equally with the law of the province in question, affirms the maxim ' Sic utere tuo ut alienum non laedas,' but the previous state of the law, whether in Quebec, or France, or England, cannot render inoperative the positive enactment of a statute, and the whole case turns, not upon what was the common law of either country, but what is the true construction of plain words authorizing the doing of the very thing complained of.	.
Therefore, the judgment of the Privy Council in that case was not to the effect of maintaining the common law, as was explained, but of maintaining the statutory law. Well, if by a statutory law a company enjoys special privileges, why not by another statutory enactment give an individual the same privileges ? In other words, I say that if you give these companies immense powers, if you give them large privileges, I do not see why you should not give the farmer, whose properties are riparian to the property of the company, the tights enjoyed by this same company.

This is not a condition that would be burdensome upon the railways. Some railways practically comply with it very fairly at the present time, and it is probably in their interest to do so. The railways in the neighbourhood where I live have been in the habit of burning the useless materials from time to time for their own protection, therefore, so far as they are concerned, I do not think this is absolutely necessary. It is 'certainly in harmony with what we have 'done this afternoon and it is not as strin-'gent, perhaps, as the provision which has *been adopted. It merely provides that if the railway company neglect to take steps to prevent fires from originating' on their property they shall be liable to the owner or occupier of the land adjoining for the damage occasioned.

I may point out to the hon. gentleman that the amendment to which he refers is no improvement upon the clause which the committee have already adopted because the amendment I moved this afternoon in a very few words covers all the hon. gentleman's motion does :
The company shall at all times maintain and [DOT] keep its right of way free and clear of all inflammable matter.
The hon. gentleman's motion differs from this in that it names the classes of inflammable matter that ought to be removed ; beyond that it does not vary. Well, the penalty clauses of the Bill apply to any infraction of this section, and if there is a continuance of such infraction of the law, from day to day, each day constitutes a distinct offence and subjects the company and its officers to a distinct penalty. I do not see any reason why the hon. gentleman should press the motion. It is true that the hon. gentleman points out that section 238 contains very much the same words, and is framed in the same manner as his motion in regard to the failure of the company to remove thistles and noxious weeds. The promoters sometimes ask bonding powers up to $20,000 a mile, and when some member of the committee asks why they wish such large bonding powers, their reply is that the country is rocky, or something of that kind. In fact, there is no information before the committee to enable the members intelligently to discuss the Bill. Under the provision I propose, parties wish-

mg to get a railway charter have to show their bona tides, in the first place, by putting up a sum of money in the hands of the railway commission to pay the cost of an investigation. The railway commission will send out an engineer to investigate whether there is any necessity for the road. If he finds that there is no necessity for it, he will so report. If he finds that there is, he will report upon the character of the country, the approximate cost of the road, whether there is any other charter for that part of the country, and whether the proposed charter is likely to interfere with vested rights. If that were done, and the report were handed to the minister and printed and placed in the hands of members when any application for a charter comes before the Railway Committee, it would enable the members to deal intelligently with the application. It would be a great improvement on the present condition of things. We are told that there is a great deal of charter-mongering going on. This would put a stop to that, because parties applying for charters would have to put up a sum of money with the railway commissioners before they could make an application at all. When parties come to this House and ask for franchises to build railroads all over the country, the government and the members of this House should know exactly what to say to those people. If some one goes to a loan company and makes an application for a loan of a sum of money, the company does not hand out the money without sending its inspector to see what the property on which the loan is to be made iis like. We should he in the same position when an application is made for a railway charter. We should know everything in regard to the character of the country and in regard to the proposed railway. If the minister and the House will accept this amendment, dt will be a big improvement on the old system.

House again in Committee of Supply.
Indians-Ontario and Quebec-further amount required for relief and medical attendance, *2,500.

['There was such a petition as my hon. friend refers to, which was sent to our agent there. He made an explanation which the deputy considered as satisfactory. If the hon. gentleman requires any further investigation, I will have it done.\nSome resolutions reported.']

About a month ago a gentleman came here from England, who was connected, I think, with the oldest society in existence having relations to the Indians on this North American continent, a society that was chartered in Cromwell's time. I was surprised to find how deep an interest they took in the Indians of this country. That gentleman came to Ottawa and called on the department, and was delighted with the reception he received. He came to Toronto with me, and I introduced him to Mr. Boyle and others interested in Indian matters. He went to Brantford and stayed there a week, studying the condition of the Indians on the Brantford reserve. He wrote me a note regretting that be was not able to come here on his return home after his visit, but saying that he was exceedingly satisfied and very much pleased with the condition of the Indians and with the care they received. But there was one point to which he took objection, and that is a point I brought up here two or three years ago at the request of a gentleman who takes great interest in them, Mr. Hamilton, of Toronto. This gentleman from England said he found on the reserve that the medical man lived miles away, that the medical man appointed a substitute who was also away from the reserve, and the substitute appointed a substitute for himself, and this latter was the only man living on the reserve to whom the Indians could go in case of sickness. He thought that was a very serious matter, and constituted a grave defect in the administration of Indian affairs, as regards that particular reserve.

I remember that the hon. gentleman brought this matter to my attention. I am not able at present to say that I have a very distinct recollection of the details which he gave me. But I can tell him now that I will give the matter immediate attention.

This gentleman who came here to visit the Indians says that the In-

dians felt keenly that they were being neglected. With this exception, he expressed the very highest approval of the administration so far as he observed it. The chief medical man, X understand, is Dr. Secord. Would the minister say what salary he gets, and what salary is paid to his deputies ?

The salary paid Dr. Secord is $2,800. He arranges for his assistants himself, and pays them out of his own salary.
Mr. OSLER, Surely that is a very unwise method. If he appoints his own assistants it may be taken for granted that they are not highly paid men. As the chief medical officer does not live on the reserve but lives twelve miles away, it is necessary that there should be an assistant. I do not think it is right that the doctor should have the appointment of his assistant when he has to pay him out of his own salary.

The difficulty mentioned by my bon. friend is not one that can be arranged very easily. It is difficult to get a medical man of good standing and ability to take up Indian work, and live upon the reserve and devote himself to it. The arrangement is the result of the experience of the department in past years, but I admit it is open to objection. I can promise the hon. member that I will see if a better arrangement can be made.
Does the assistant not live upon the reserve ?
Under the arrangement be is required to live upon the reserve.

But I understand that he does not live on the reserve. I hold that a medical man twelve miles away cannot take proper care of the Indians in case of sickness, and the case is still worse when the assistant is away. This is not a thing that can be farmed out with good results, because the party who hires the assistant has in all probability a very large rake-off. Therefore, the assistant will do his work in a perfunctory manner, and as little of it as possible.
The minister forgot to tell us whether these assistants are duly qualified practitioners.
The assistant is a qualified practitioner.

Does the hon. minister think it is acting with prudence as regards these people to leave it in such a position that the medical officer draws a salary of $2,800 a year ? He farms it out to a regular practitioner who does not permanently reside upon the reserve and that gentleman has the right to send students to look after Mr. OSLER.
the Indians and take his place. It comes down to this that we are paying $2,800 a year, probably not too much for this service, which in the end is performed by students.

The hon. gentleman is under a misapprehension in regard to the payment of the salary. The payment is made out of the Indian fund and with the consent of the band. The arrangement is approved by the band that pays the money. The department has not received any complaints from the Indians. Notwithstanding that, I quite admit that it is an arrangement that requires to be looked into and fully considered.

I spoke from the statement that this gentleman made to me after he had been nearly a week on the reserve. The complaints came directly from the Indians to him. This gentleman, Mr. Wigram, was nearly a week on the reserve observing for himself. He was exceedingly pleased with everything in connection with the baud and the one complaint of the Indians was that they were neglected in their medical attendance. He found that the doctor who is in charge'does not live upon the reserve. His deputy was away for an indefinite period and his deputy had appointed a deputy to act for him while he was away. That deputy may have been a student, and if he was a student he probably would be appointed without pay. While it is quite true that Dr. Secord draws money that may come from the Indian fund, I do not think , that is a reason why the money should not be properly administered. I am glad that the hon. minister says that he will take the matter up. I think he will find that the case is as I have stated, and that the condition of the medical service on the reserve is not satisfactory.

I do not want the hon. minister to understand me as complaining about the amount. I merely suggested that the person who is performing the service is not probably receiving the money, and therefore, the service would not be performed so well. Even if the government were directly paying the money, if more money were required I would not have any complaint to make at all.

I would regard the plan as a very bad one for more reasons than one. The first reason is that it is very improper for a medical man to farm out work of that kind, and money spent in that way is not wisely spent. The second is that the poor Indian is paying out of this fund a consideration for proper medical attendance which he is not getting. It is said that the assistant resides on the reserve but the complaint of the Indians was that the assistant was away for several weeks and that he sent a substitute in his place. Who is the substitute ? He is likely to be a student

of one or two years standing, who takes this opportunity of acquiring some knowledge of practice, because lie lias no legal right to practice except by going to see a patient under some medical man and tliat medical man could not charge for that service if the patient disputed the bill. But he is not in the proper sense a practitioner and the Indian is obliged to depend upon the service of a student, who perhaps has no proper knowledge of his profession at all. Now, the original practitioner receives a large amount of money out of the Indian fund. He gets $2,800 a year, when in reality the Indian may not have $100 worth of service from the medical branch, because the service of a student of one or two years standing would not be regarded amongst civilized and intelligent people in any portion of this country as a proper practice of the profession, nor would it be regarded as a fulfilment of a contract to provide medical attendance on a railway or a public work.

Who is the agent at the St. Peters' reserve in Manitoba ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
The Rev. John Semmens.

What is his age ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
I have not the record just at hand, but he is a man of fifty-two or fifty-three.

Does he live on the reserve, or how far away from it ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
His instructions are that he has to live on the reserve. I believe he does so.

Is there a general controller or commissioner who has supervision of the agents like this gentleman, Mr. Bell, in that district ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
The general inspector of the district is Mr. S. .1. Jackson, of Stonewall.
How old is he ?
About fifty-five.

I do not think that we have properly finished the subject. Since it has been brought to the attention of the hon. minister is he not prepared to say that he will discontinue a system so unjust and improper, because, it seems to me as a medical man, that it is a very great injustice to the Indians.

The question of medical attendance upon Indians is always a difficult question. You never can satisfy Indians that they are being properly attended to medically. The more medical attendance that is provided the more they want. Their demands grow in
proportion to the supply, and it is always a very difficult matter to satisfy Indians upon that particular question. As hon. gentlemen can see the tendency is towards growth in the expenditure for medical attendance. It is difficult to get a good practitioner to reside on the reserve and devote himself to it. I am not satisfied that the arrangement upon the reserve is not a fairly good one ; at the same time I am quite satisfied after all that has been said that this is a subject for careful consideration.
I am satisfied that there is an objection to the system of allowing a physician to employ his own agent and to fix the remuneration. I appreciate fully the force of what hon. gentlemen have said and I will look into the matter and see if any improvement can be made.

Does the hon. minister think that if he finds this case as I have stated it he might give a promise that the pay of the physician shall be made through the government and not. through the head man who lives twelve or fifteen miles away from the reserve ? You can never have a system satisfactory to the Indians until that is done. There is no consideration required on that point at all.
My hon. friend will hardly ask me to make a positive promise that a change will be inade until I know it can be carried out.

Three years ago the complaint was made and the minister promised that he would look into it. To-night that complaint is made stronger than ever. It is so manifest that the system is wrong that it requires no considration at all.
I went over the whole matter very carefully with the medical gentleman at the time and no complaint has been made since. I was under the impression that everything was satisfactory.
Such a system could not be satisfactory.

The Indians are paying sufficient money to have a qualified medical man to attend them. Two thousand eight hundred dollars a year is a very good salary for that kind of practice. The system of farming out a practice is bad, because the person who is employed usually gets a small salary and is liable to do his work in a perfunctory manner. No medical man should be allowed to attend the Indians unless he is duly certified to practice in any *part of the country. The medical man should be a lawfully qualified practitioner and not a student who perhaps may have little knowledge of his profession. I admit that it is the experience of medical men that it is hard to please the Indians and 'that sometimes they think they are sick when they are not sick at all, but an in-

telligent practitioner can easily discover that and should tell the Indian that he is hot sick if such be the case. I am told that they are sometimes put off with a dose of salts, which if it does not do them any good 'will not do them any harm, but even that is 'not a good system. A medical man who thoroughly knows his profession ought to have dignity and confidence enough in himself to tell the Indian that he does not require medicine if such be the case. If you allow such a system to continue on the Indian reserves you are liable to get quacks or 'charlatans when the Indians are paying enough money to get a qualified practitioner. The minister must see that the system is bad and he should at once make a change.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item be adopted.

No. If the minister does hot give us an answer we must insist on knowing what he is going to do before the item is passed. The minister might as well understand early as late that we will not be treated as if we had no rights in this House.

The hon. gentleman knows that he cannot expect me to give a positive promise now.
1 can tell him that I will recommend such a change as will seem to me to be desirable in the line of a complete and satisfactory medical attendance. There are a great 'many Indian reserves in Canada and I cannot be expected to have intimate knowledge of the details of what is going on in each reserve. The matter was gone into carefully some years ago and inasmuch as the Inspector of the Indian agencies has not called my attention to any complaints since that time, it was reasonable to expect that the matters, were then placed on a satisfactory basis. I am informed that the department has no reason to suppose that the medical service has been inefficient. There was an outbreak of small-pox in that reserve last year and I am informed that it was handled with great skill and was stamped out in a very short time. I will look into the matter carefully and I will make the best arrangement I can.

Is it not reasonable to expect that the minister will say that the medical attendants on these reserves shall be properly qualified practitioners. There is no family in this country who is paying for a doctor and who would be treated by physicians who are not duly qualified. The minister ought at least to be prepared to say that he will supply properly qualified physicians to these Indians. As to whether he should live on the reserve or off it, it 'seems to me that it does not require very great intelligence to discern how difficult it would be for a medical man living twelve miles from the reserve to do Justice to the Indians. It would put the Indians to a 'great deal of inconvenience in eases of em-

ergency, or at certain seasons of the year when the roads are bad; whereas a medical man living on the reserve would be available at an hour's notice. I think it is not too much to ask the hon. gentleman to see that, as the Indian fund provides sufficient to give the Indians a properly qualified practitioner, they should have one.

l.1 s?ve ^le promise the hon. gentleman asks, it might involve the prohibition of medical students going on the reserve at all to assist in attending to the Indians, and I do not know that that would be a good thing. I may say to my hon. friend that the medical practitioner on the reserve has to be appointed with the consent of the council of the band, which is composed of men of a considerable degree of intelligence, who know what should be done in a case of that kind. To make the change proposed might involve bringing some of the Indians down here to consult with them. I would rather put myself in the position of not making the promise than to make it, and not be able to carry it out. All I can say is that I will do the best I can, both for the Indians and with the fund.

I would submit to the hon. minister this question in his own case; if he were sending for a medical man to whom he was paying a good fee for his services, and some student who might not have studied for two years were sent to him, would he be satisfied to pay for the services of that student as much as he would for the services of a well qualified medical man? The same rule ought to apply to the Indians who are paying out of their fund the full compensation for the attendance of a well qualified medical man. We a,re told that even the assistant was not on the reserve for a week, but sent another to do his work, and that :is what we complain of. So far as we know, there is no properly qualified medical man to do the work. If the work must be farmed out, it should at least be given to a professional man who understands his business, because full compensation is being paid for the attendance of such a man.
Is this man allowed also to attend to other practice in Brantford ?
Yes.

Does not the hon. minister think that is unfair to the other practitioners in the city of Brantford ? Does he not think that it is a reasonable request that this man, who is paid $2,800 a year for attending the Indians, should not be allowed to interfere with the practice of the other physicians in the city of Brantford ? If this were done, this man would be able to give to the Indians the properl attendance they require. Will the minister*

promise that he will see that this physician shall not be permitted to engage in other practice than among the Indians ?

I am afraid I cannot promise that. As to the effect on the other physicians in the city of Brantford, all I can say is that I have never looked at the matter from that standpoint. I have been administering the affairs of the department for the benefit of the Indians. I do not know that it is a serious matter to the other physicians in the city of Brantford that he gets a salary. I have never heard a complaint raised on their behalf until my hon. friend has raised it to-night. I have discussed this subject quite frequently with my hon. friend from South Brant (Mr. Heyd), who I am glad to see here, and who is perhaps more familiar with the reserve than any one else, and I have never heard that point raised in my conversations with him. In nine cases out of ten, the Indian physicians will find that the work they do for the Indians is a small part of their practice. In some places it is a small part, and in other places a large part; but I doubt very much if it is practicable to carry out the principle which the hon. gentleman suggests.

I do not mean that it should apply to all the physicians attending Indians. In cases where the salary is very small, it would hardly be expected; but in a case like this, where the medical man is receiving a salary of $2,800 a year, I think the minister might fairly apply the principle; because there is no doubt that this man has a decided advantage over the other physicians practicing in Brantford. When was he appointed to this position ?
The exact date is not to hand at present, but it was about six years ago.
Was he appointed at the same salary, or has it been increased since ?
The same salary.

In this case the hon. minister is deviating from another principle that was adopted by hon. gentlemen opposite not only when in opposition, but since the present government came into power. I know that when hon. gentlemen opposite were in opposition, they objected to any physician practicing who held a government appointment. Let me cite the instance of the physicians in the Kingston penitentiary. When that appointment was given to Dr. Phelan, he had to give up his practice, and although he was one of the leading physicians in Kingston he accepted a position at $1,800 a year, and gave up his other practice. Why, therefore, is this physician in Brantford allowed to practice in opposition to the other physicians in that
town ? I ask that he be put into the same position as other physicians who have been given government appointments, and be compelled to give up his other practice.

I was not present when this discussion began and do not know just what has been said, but I can plead a legitimate excuse because I was attending the redistribution committee, giving some testimony with regard to a matter of considerable importance to myself. As I have personal knowledge of the facts, I would ask permission of the House to explain this matter. I can do so all the more strenuously because I believe that the present conditions, under which our Indian friends are supplied with doctors, are the best that can be devised. I have no personal interest at stake, and am simply influenced by my regard for the welfare of the Indians. There is one objection to having the Indian physician a resident on the reserve. You cannot get a first-class man to go there with his family, because there is no social intercourse for his wife and no suitable schools for his children. For these reasons a first-class man will not go and live there for the salary, although it appears high to some hon. gentlemen opposite. You must have a married man to begin with. That is absolutely necessary on the reserve. In order that these four thousand Indians should be provided with proper medical attendance, you must have a first-class man, a married man, who is conscientious and whose moral character is beyond reproach. In order that these people should be properly treated, that doctor must have a qualified assistant, who will look after the ordinary cases of disease while he attends to the most serious ones. The present physician, Dr. Secord, has a qualified assistant, who is also a married man and who lives on the reserve constantly and is, therefore, in close touch with the people.
What is his name ?

He is a son of the gentleman who represents Haldimand in the local legislature. His name is Holmes. He is a qualified doctor and is constantly on the reserve. He was a student who had just passed and was about qualifying for his degree, when he was given this position by Dr. Secord. There is, therefore, not much left out of his government salary, after Dr. Secord pays this young man who is his assistant. The reserve covers some sixty-four square miles, and the physician's practice requires some rough driving, which an ordinary physician has not the slightest conception of. I do not think that the Indians could have a better doctor than Dr. Secord. All the serious cases he looks after himself personally, and is recognized as eminently well qualified to do so, and he has a qualified man to look after the others. Dr. Secord drives to the reserve, some four or five times a week, stays there

over night, and looks after the more serious cases, while his assistant, who is a qualified physician, looks after the others. I do not know how the Indians could be better served. I can testify to the conscientious way in which the physicians discharge their duty. If you were to limit Dr. Secord to his practice on the reserve, he would not take the position nor would any other physician of his standing, because there would not be enough money in it left, after paying for the three horses which he requires in order to attend properly to the work. Our Indians are being better served by their physicians to-day than they were ever before. Their hygienic condition is being constantly improved under the wise supervision ' of Dr. Secord and bis assistant, and any charges made against him have been simply evolved out of political consideration.
He is quite a politician.

He was until he was appointed, but since then he does not meddle with politics ; and I can say, to the credit of all the civil servants in Brantford, that they are absolutely loyal to the men who pay them, and leave politics alone. The best proof of that is the fact that when this government assumed office, the civil servants were all Conservatives in the town of Brantford, and not one of them has been removed.

The hon. gentleman states that the reason why it was necessary to employ Dr. Secord is because it required an upright and honourable man to fill the position, and it was impossible to get a man of that kind to live on the reserve.

I did not say that.
Mr-. REID (Grenville). The hon. gentleman said it would be impossible to get a first-class practitioner and an upright, honourable man to live on the reserve. I think that that is a very unfair reflection on Dr. Holmes, who is living on the reserve and who is a married man. Surely it is hardly fair that the hon. gentleman should thus reflect on the character of Dr. Holmes, who is living there with his family. If this Dr. Holmes is qualified to practice on the reserve, and if he be an upright and honourable man and is willing to live on the reserve, he should get the salary for doing the work; and if so, I am sure he would not try to do any outside practice.

The hon. member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd) says the physicians in Brantford do not object to this arrangement. He knows very well that if he recommended Dr. Secord for the position, as no doubt he did, it would be useless for any physician in Brantford to object to Dr. Secord, because his objection would be taken no notice of. The hon. minister states that it is impossible to get a qualified practitioner to live among the Indians and attend to them. And now the hon. member for South Brant tells us that there is a qualified practitioner living among the Indians and attending to them, and doing the work well. This gentleman is doing all the work, but he has to give up a certain amount of his salary to Dr. Secord, for he knows that if he did not do so he could not hold the position. So long as Dr. Secord .wishes to take the bonus, the other man must pay it and say nothing, or he will lose the position. The other physicians of Brantford, whether Liberals or Conservatives, know that it would be useless to enter any protest. It is the duty of the hon. member for South Brant to protect the other physicians in Brantford instead of trying to give this one man a bonus by farming-out this position. Where the government pay a sufficient salary for the physician to do this work, that salary should go to the man who is doing the work, and another physician should not take a bonus from the man who actually does the work. It is quite true that there might be serious cases in which a consultation would be required. In that case, the doctor on the reserve could call in Dr. Secord or any other person he wished, and pay him a fee out of his salary. But I think it is most unfair that the man who is doing the work should only receive a small portion of the salary. I am not reflecting on Dr. Secord ; I do not know that gentleman at all. I have no doubt that he is the best physician in Brantford. But what I object to is his being allowed to hold this position and farming it out in this way, thus getting a bonus to compete against other doctors in his city. The gov-

eminent themselves have set a precedent in the case of Dr. Phelan, who was appointed physician to the Kingston penitentiary. He is not allowed to practice. Why then, should this physician be allowed to practice outside of the position he has. I do not think it is unfair to ask that the position should be given to some one, Dr. Secord or any other, I have no objection to Dr. Secord-with the understanding that he is to live on the reserve as Dr. Holmes does, and attend to the Indians.

It is a curious thing that the one who lives in Brantford, knows the doctors In the city, knows the circumstances of the ease, knows exactly the political effect upon himself if he offends the doctors of that city, or if he does not do the best thing in the interest of the citizens and the Indians, is to be instructed by a gentleman who lives two hundred miles away, who knows nothing of the conditions, and represents no grievance. If the doctors do hot like the arrangement I am pretty sure to hear of it; if the Indians do not like it, they will not keep that fact to themselves; and if the gentleman on the reserve does not like it I am sure he will very soon tell me so. But there is no dissatisfaction. The man on the reserve is getting the wages to be given him by Dr. Secord, which is a large portion of the salary. If lie got the appointment he would have to employ some one to relieve him of a certain portion of the labour. The Indians have the advice and constant supervision of one of the ablest and most experienced physicians in Brantford, the constant attendance of Dr. Holmes, the attendance at times of students and a great deal of medicine, all for $2,800.

The hon. member for South Brant was not present when I brought this matter up. I explained that a gentleman of high position in England, Mr. Wigram, who is much interested in Indian affairs, came with a letter to me. I tried to find the hon. member for South Brant here, as I told Mr. Wigram that that hon. gentleman would put him on the track of getting the information he wanted. Mr. Wigram went to Brantford and spent some days on the reserve. One of his objects was to find out whether the funds of the Indians were being wasted or not. He afterwards Wrote me from New York, expressing regret that he could not come back this way and telling me that he was highly pleased with everything he saw on the reserve except one point which he thought ought to be remedied. He found that the doctor lived miles away, that the doctor appointed a substitute, but that substitute was not then on the reserve and was away for an indefinite period, and had in turn appointed a substitute. This was one thing that caused dissatisfaction among the Indians. And it appears to me quite clear that this is a thing that ought to be remedied. I realize that it might be difficult to get the con-1 199
suiting physician to live upon the reserve. But I do contend that the pay of the man who lives upon the reserve should be made direct from the Indian Department and not from a local doctor. The natural tendency of a doctor in such a case would be to get the service done as cheaply as possible. The Minister of the Interior said it was impossible to get a qualified man to live on the reserve. I agreed with him that it was a difficult thing. But the member for Brantford (Mr. Heyd) says there is a most respectable and well qualified man living on the reserve with his family. That does away with the only answer the minister could give.

Dr. Holmes is a young physician who has not had the necessary experience to take supervision over a large reserve like that. I do not know what he gets. He gets the house he lives in, and I think he gets $1,200 or 1,500 a year. I do not think there is more than $1,000 left for Dr. Secord.
Will the minister' say that he will give Dr. Holmes the position, or else ask Dr. Secord to live on the reserve ?

In the first place I did not say that there was not a qualified practitioner on the reserve. I said that the assistant who lived on the reserve was a qualified practitioner. I have stated also at the beginning of the discussion, that it was difficult to get a qualified man to live on the reserve, and my hon. friend from Brantford has explained why, and he has fuller knowledge of the matter than I have. I am not prepared to say that I will make any change in the arrangement in that respect, but I will look into the matter and see if any improvement can be made.
Who was the physician previous to Dr. Secord ?

Dr. Langrel was appointed by the late government. He discharged the duties for a good many years, until finally he got tired and resigned and went to Hamilton to live. He left the reserve in charge of his two sons, young men who had not had much experience. The present government appointed Dr. Secord, who was appointed before I entered the House.
Were these two young men qualified practitioners when they were on the reserve ?

They had no regular status there, they were simply discharging the work of their father who had left the reserve. Dr. Secord employed several gentlemen to assist him until finally he got Dr. Holmes, who has had much experience, who is respectable and qualified, and in a few years will be able to take charge of the
4,000	people, when he also will have to em-

ploy an assistant. By that time very likely Dr. Secord will have resigned the job, and I shall be happy to recommend Dr. Holmes.
I see in addition to Dr. Second's salary that he gets $2,055 for extras.

No, $300 for special medicine. He supplies all the drugs for the whole of that reserve. When they want castor oil to grease their wagons they generally go to the doctor and get it. These Indians want expensive drugs, they want quinine. The government allows $300 for medical supplies, and they cost about $600.
On the one side there seems to be a complaint from the Indians as voiced through the gentleman referred to by the hon. gentleman from West Toronto.
The Indians are not complaining. _
But the hon. member from West Toronto gave the testimony of a gentleman saying they were complaining.

You must bear in mind the conditions under which he visited the reserve and the short time he was there. At present there is very little sickness on the reserve, as there seldom is in the summer time.

The Indians complain that Dr. Secord, who receives a large salary, farms out the work to another gentleman, to Dr. Holmes, but the trouble does not end there, because Dr. Holmes won't stay on the reserve, and he farms out the work to another gentleman, who, when he gets weary, goes over to Brantford, and the consequence is that the Indians are left without any physician. Now on referring to the Auditor General's Beport, I find that this Dr. L. Secord, when he does not want to go down to the reserve to attend to the duties for which he is paid $2,800, he sends down Dr. E. R. Secord, his partner, I suppose.
That is his son who had just graduated from McGill College.
And living at home with his father.

And who took five first class scholarships. He was employed by the Indian Department to go down and stamp out a small-pox epidemic on the reserve. The city of Brantford employed him to do the same thing in Brantford. As Dr. Secord could not expose himself to the contagion of small-pox and visit the rest of the Indians he hired his son to do that, and he stamped out the small-pox on the reserve in about four weeks.
I thought the objection that had been made by the hon. gentleman to the other doctor was" that he was a young man and now he is backing up the employment of a young man without experience.
Could you expect the doctor to expose himself to small-pox and then look after the other Indians on the reserve ?
The hon. gentleman objected that Dr. Second's substitute was a young man living on the reserve and that he had no experience.
Dr. Secord could not attend to the small-pox patients and look after the other Indians as well.

I am not objecting- to that. This is a question of experience. An epidemic of. small-pox is a very serious thing, but while the hon. gentleman says that it is wise and defensible to send a man just fresh from McGill who has taken half a dozen medals and scholarships and who is certainly a gentleman of not much experience to stamp out an epidemic of small-pox he objects to the other young man because of the lack of experience.
The best evidence of his ability is that he cured all the people of small-pox and stamped the disease out of the reserve.

In about four weeks. There were about twenty Indians ill with smallpox, they were all isolated and had to be taken care of in tents, they were nil cured and the small-pox was stamped out of the reserve. It is more difficult to treat Indians in cases of this kind than whites, because the Indians are less careful. .

I think it is rather bard on the funds of this Indian tribe that they should be encroached upon by the rapacity of this Secord family. First, there is Dr. Secord, sr., with $2,800 a year and $300 extra. He does not like to go down to the reserve because there is a contagious disease there, and so he farms it out to Dr. Secord, jr., and the young man picks up no less a sum than $810 for his services. I suppose he was at home enjoying a holiday. It turned out at the expense of the Indians to be a very profitable one to him. the department, what do the department do ? They simply graft the Secord family and the rest of these Grit physicians, as I suppose they are all friends of the hon. member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd)

There is this in it.
