Hear, hear.-

What has been said on the other side of the House is the result of an absolute want of knowledge of the facts of the case. The character of Dr. Seeord and his family has been aspersed by men who know nothing about him.

I said nothing about Dr. Seeord, but I said that the Indians were dissatisfied. I said that Dr. Seeord was a most active politician, and the member for Brantford and the Minister of Customs will not deny that.
He was mayor of the city of Brantford.
He was a very prominent politician.
A most respected gentleman.
I did not asperse Dr. Second's character except it be an aspersion on his character to say that he is a prominent Liberal.
This ' rapacious Seeord family ! '
Well, when he gets $2,800 a year and when he did not give a
little patronage to some other Liberal doctor in his city but gave it to his own son, It shows that there was at least a good greed about it.

I havei heard nothing said which would prove to my satisfaction that Dr. Second has not performed his duties properly. It is true that a complaint was made to a medical gentleman who visited the reserve, and when that' complaint was called to my attention by a respected member of the House, I at once said that I would have it looked into. I do not for a moment admit that that complaint indicates that there is any defect in the medical attendance on the reserve. I know something about Indians, and I can say that it is probable that if a visit were made to any reserve under such circumstances, it is likely that complaints would be made which might not on investigation be well founded. I will not admit that Dr. Seeord was in any respect neglectful of his duties. I simply say that I will investigate the complaint and see if there is any improvement to make. For some years I have had to administer matters relating to quarantine, and the result of my experience leads me to be very greatly surprised at the fact that upon this reserve, with an outbreak of thirty-three cases of small-pox, the entire expense of coping with it was only $4,600, in addition to the ordinary medical expense. Any person who has experience will say that this was a phenomenally low charge for handling such an outbreak. My hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) and other members who have had experience in matters of tnis kind, will agree with me in that statement. Furthermore, the men in charge of this matter are perfectly competent. Mr. Cameron, the Indian agent has experience since his appointment in 1891, and he is one of the best and most competent and reliable agents in the service. Mr. Cameron had entire charge of what was done there for the department. It was his business to see that no unnecessary expenditure was incurred. Let me tell my hon. friends that upon this reserve there is a board of health, composed of very intelligent members of the Indian tribe ; there is also an Indian council, and they supervise, along with our officers, the work of this quarantine and the payment of the accounts by the government. No complaint has reached the department in regard to the amounts paid. Mr. Cameron, if it amounts to anything, is not a politician of the government, but a man appointed by our predecessors. We have him, we have the medical superintendent, we have the Indian board of health, we have the Indian council, and not one of these has made a complaint. My hon. friends may rest easy that in that respect' their anxiety as to Indian funds are not well founded.

It Is a new doctrine to me that we are to be criticised because we see fit to challenge the estimates of any minister in this House. What are the facts of the case ? I could not help admiring how sincere our hon. friend from South Brant (Mr. Heyd) was. He was so sincere, and he was so sincere. It put me in mind of what I used to hear, that we always had suspicion of people who protested so much.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) Louder.

Well, just possess your soul in patience. My voice is my own, and I will use it as I like.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) It is very squeaky.

And if the hon. gentleman does not want to hear, there is a door, and he can walk out. The facts of the case are these. The Indian fund was used to pay a physician. He is eminent, I daresay, and he got $2,800 to attend to the medical wants of that tribe of Indians. We had to have an old experienced man, because a young man. Dr. Holmes, was not competent. I think Dr. Holmes should have that money. He has passed his medical examination, he is married and is living on the reserve. I repudiate the idea that a man requires to be an old fogey to be a qualified medical man. In my part of the country it is the young men who are generally the up-to-date clever men, while the old fogeys are not up-to-date. Dr. Holmes is living on the reserve, and is attending to the Indians as well as he can. When a critical case arose he was sent down and it cost $800 more, as 1 understand, in consequence. And yet my hon. friend from South Brant says that our friends who are living 200 miles away should not say anything about it. But we never entered a protest when the hon. gentleman from British Columbia, who lives
3,000	miles away, came to the hon. gentleman's relief. He was then as mild and meek as a sucking baby. What more do we want than we find in the records of the Auditor General's Report ? When there was a serious case on the reserve, and an old experienced man was wanted to attend to it, a young man just fresh from college was sent to attend to the case, and the hon. gentleman said, we are satisfied. If we were in control of the government and were doing such a job. would he have been satisfied ? He would have said it was bribery and corruption. You know deep down in your hearts that you have gone back on everything you advocated in opposition. I want the Minister of Customs to mention one principle that he supported when in opposition that he has not violated.
I will not take up the time of the committee in recounting all the principles that we have kept. That would take too long.
You could do it in five minutes.

It is well to have criticisms of these accounts ; we do not object to that But perhaps the criticisms of lion, gentlemen opposite are not so much required in this instance as they will be when we come to items involving the expenditure of the people's money by this government. These accounts have been paid out of the Indians' money.
Therefore you would let people steal it.

And they have passed an audit, quite as intelligent an audit as that which is being bestowed upon it here, judging from the remarks of some of the gentlemen. This account came before the council of the Six Nation Indians. It is their money, and they are particular how their money shall be expended. They are the ones who made the request and who pay the accounts. When an account comes before them, they scrutinize it. That was done in this case. They saw that the account was right, and they sent it to the government and asked that it be paid. And after all that has been done, some hon. gentlemen in this House feel it incumbent upon them to rise and criticise this account. There are items to come to which criticism might be devoted, which have not passed the scrutiny of any auditing body. But this item has passed the scrutiny of the auditing body that pays the money, and they themselves ask us to pay it. The minister tells me, and I have no doubt he is correct, that lie has had no representations from the Indians at all against this arrangement in regard to the medical attendance on the reserve. Any one acquainted with the Indian character, and who knows the independence of the Six Nation Indians, as I do, knows very well that if there is any cause of complaint it is not long before the department hears of it. In a case of this kind, where there are
3,000	or 4,000 Indians governed by a council of very intelligent men, many of them educated, when they have expressed no dissatisfaction, I cannot see that there can be any strong criticism lodged against this expenditure or against anything connected with the medical attendance of the Six Nation Indians. It is their own money, they audit it, and it would not be paid without their sanction.
If they are so intelligent and so well able to look after their 'own interests, why not allow them to select their own physician ?
Their *physician is not forced upon them.

You appoint him.

' The MINISTER OF CUSTOMS. Certainly, under an arrangement between the government and the Indians, who are their Wards, but the government do not over-ride the Indian council; and if any representations were made to the government by the council, through the Indian agent, that the Indians were not satisfied, the minister would look into them. No complaint however has ever been made, and hou. geutie-inen opposite evidently do not understand the question. But no doubt there are some Items in the estimates upon which they will be able to do a little better.
The position which the hon. minister takes is hardly fair. He knows that the government appoint the physician and that the Indians must accept him.

But as Dr. Holmes is doing this work for $1,200 as stated by the hou. member for Brant
I do not know what he gets.

Why not give him the position as a small increase on the salary he is now getting and allow the Indians to benefit by the amount paid Dr. Secord for services he is really not performing. I do not know how long it lasted. I thought that Dr. Secord was getting $50 a week, and if he was paid $800, that represented sixteen weeks.
He was getting $10 a day, and was paid for eighty-one days. That was three and one-half months, which the small-pox epidemic must have lasted.

Mr. REID (Grenville)). It is very nearly three months. At any rate it is much longer than the hon. member for Brant stated. And there is hardly any small-pox epidemic which lasts much longer than about

Last year there was a small-pox epidemic all over the west and we had a great deal of expense and trouble in connection with it. Up to date the expenditure has been $8,000 with some accounts still to come in. We estimate $10,000 for that. Then, there is $5,000 for the relief of Indians outside the treaty limits." The estimates for the liscal year 1902-3 did not contain an item for this service, possibly because of oversight on the part of officers of the department. The demands made upon the department for Indians for whom they had not funds have increased. We have $5,000 in the main estimates for this year, and this $5,000 is a corresponding item for last year. The Hudson's Bay Company have paid for the relief from their posts in the north $3,000 and the total accounts are expected to amount to $5,000. The next item is $6,000 which arises in this way :	When we make
our estimates for supplies of beef to furnish the Indians, we base them upon the prices which the officers of the department estimate will have to be paid. But, last jrear the prices went up before the contract was let, and there is a difference of about $6,000 which we have to provide for. Then there is $1,070 to pay the Indians of the Qu'Ap-pelle district for loss they sustained through the burning of their threshing machines and a certain amount of wheat.
The Indians on this reserve are the best Indians in the North-west Territories. They are under the charge of an extremely efficient agent, and they follow agriculture to a much greater extent than any other Indians. They purchased a threshing machine with their own money, and last year I think they raised about 47,000 bushels of wheat. They are the most progressive Indians we have. They suffered an accident in the burning of their threshing machine, and the agent recommended that we should give them a small sum to recompense them for the loss they had sustained, and this the department decided to do. Then there is an item of $3,000 required for these purposes. We had to send out a commission to settle the half-breed claims under treaty No. 8. Treaty No. 8 is a new treaty with the In-

dians in the district north of Edmonton, where we have within the last two or three years brought the Indians under treaty limits and obtained possession of the territory. We send out a man every year to make payments. The commission went out for the purpose of settling with the halfbreeds and to issue scrip two or three years ago. In the first place, the country is of vast extent, and the population is scattered. When the commission went up there for the purpose of taking evidence with regard to the half-breed claims, some of the halfbreeds were away hunting and fishing in different parts of the country, they did not all get there, and another officer went next year to take evidence. There are still some left, and for the purpose of clearing them all up we send this officer up there. I do not think it is likely we shall have to send him again. Another item is for the purpose of paying the salary of the medical officer. There is no physician resident in that whole country. One of the arrangements that was made at the time the treaty was entered into with the Indians was that when we sent our officer up there to pay the treaty money we would send a medical man along with him, so that when the Indians came to receive their money, if there were any among them seriously ill, they could bring them there to receive medical treatment at the same time. That was a stipulation specially made at the time the treaty was entered into. That is one of the things to which the Indians attach the most importance, and which we have endeavoured to carry out as well as we can. It is difficult to get a medical man to go there, and we have made an arrangement with an officer of the mounted police who is acquainted with the country, who is also a competent medical man, and knows the Indians very well, hence a very desirable man. He has undertaken to perform this service if we give him a special vote of $1,200 a year for that purpose. We cannot expect any man to undertake such a duty unless we give him a liberal allowance, because it involves a long and dangerous journey. After a good deal of discussion we made an arrangement with Dr. West to undertake that work, and in pursuance of the arrangement we are paying him $1,000 for ten months' service to June 30,1903. Then there is a sum of $500 for the purpose of paying a veterinary inspector of cattle. I may say that in the last five or six years we have succeeded in getting the Indians to go into cattle raising, they take much more kindly to cattle raising than to wheat raising. Their herds have now reached such an extent that we find it necessary to have the veterinary go around and make an inspection of the herds every year.
Sometimes they kill their cattle and eat them.

There have been a few cases of that kind, Hon. Mr. SIFTON.
but on the whole, if the hon. gentleman will look at the report of the Indian Department this year he will find that the improvement they have made is very gratifying, especially in those cases where we have endeavoured to introduce cattle. Some bands of Indians' have absolutely refused to undertake agriculture of the ordinary kind, but they take very kindly to cattle raising. I think that as a result of the introduction of cattle raising among them, in the course of six or seven years we will be able to dispense with rations altogether. The next item is $600 for the purpose of increasing the salary of the inspector who goes north for the purpose of paying the Indians under treaty No. 8. He has been receiving $1,200, and I think lie ought to receive $1,800. He has proved himself a competent man to do that work. I did not feel disposed to recommend an increase of his salary until*he had performed-the work at least once, and he having done so, we find that he is quite competent. That makes up the total of $25,000 for which the hon. gentleman asked .explanations.

Has the minister's attention been directed to a petition from the Indians on the St. John river and the St. Mary's river ? They sent a petition complaining of the management of their affairs. As to the merits of the petition 1 am not prepared to speak. The chief took a trip down to Ottawa clothed in the uniform of his office. I would urge the minister to look into the petition.

There was such a petition as my hon. friend refers to, which was sent to our agent there. He made an explanation which the deputy considered as satisfactory. If the hon. gentleman requires any further investigation, I will have it done.
